DER OAK UND DER VINE. I don'd vas preaching voman's rightds, • Or anvding like dot; Und I likes to see all beoples Shust gondented mit dheir lot; Budt I vants to g,ondradict dot shap . Dot made dis leedle shoke : "A voman vas der gli.,ging vine, Und man, der shturdy oak." r Berhaps, soroedimes, dot may pe drue ; Budt, den dimes oudt off nine, I find me oudt dot man himself Vas peen der plinging vine; Und ven hees frendts dile,' all vas gone, Und he vas shust " tead proke," Dot's vhen der voman shteps righdt in, Und peen der shturdy oak. ` Shust go oup to der pa,se-pall groundts Und see dhose "shturdy oaks" All planted roundt übon der seats— Shust hear dheir laughs und shokes! Dhen see dhose vomens at der tubs, Mit glothes oudt on der lines: Thich vas der shturdy oaks, mine frendts, Und vhich der glinging vines? Then Sickness in der househollt comes, Und veeks und veeks he shtays, Who vas id fighdts him mitoudt resdt, Dhose veary nighdts und days? Who beace und gomfort alvays prings, Und cools dot fefered prow? More like id vas der tender vine • Dot oak he glings to, now. "Man vants budt leedle here pelow," Der boet von time said; Dhere's leedle dot man he don'd vant, I clink id means, inslited ; Und vhen der years keep rolling on, Dheir cares und droub!es pringing, He vants to pe der shturdy oak, Und, also, do der glinging. Maype, vhen oak sdhey c.,ding some more, thid don'd so shturdy peen, Der glinging vines dhey liaf some shance To helb run Life's masheen. In belt mid sickness, ahoy und pain, In calm or slitormv veddher, 'Tvas bedcliier dot dose oaks und vines Should alvays gling togedder. CHARLES FOLLEN ADAILS.

THE MISER. A famine raged upon the hanks of Nile; The people groaned from scarcity cf corn, And that grim reaper, Death, his sickle swept Across the parched earth, no other harvest yielding Rat what he gathered with his grizzly hand. 'The little food that still remained in store Became as precious as its weight in gold; And avaricious merchants hoarded wheat lb "Joseph's granaries," against the time When the most wealthy would their dross lay down In largest heaps; their span of life to make 'The longer by the purchase of that seed, So lightly cherished in prosperity. Chief of these trafficers, the mi.Or Amin Sad gathered plenteously the golden grain; And day by day he sat upon the steps ln front of the gran'ry door, his lean old hands Within each other clasped, as if for warmth, Whilst inwardly he gloated on his stock; And, with his sunken eyes peering around ikon the wasting people. seemed to guess What untold wealth must soon be brought to him. At length no corn was elsewhere to be found, And famished crowds surrounded Amin's store, Beseeching, him to sell for charity. They laid their gold before him—precious heaps— Whereon he feasted with his eager eyes; Then slowly he unclosed his iron doors. But, lo! Recoiling from his treasury, He cried as blasted with the lightning stroke; For where had been the piles of yellow wheat A festering mass of rottenness appeared, And worms were holding highest carnival. Starving, the people; yet they loudly raised A shout of triumph at the judgment dire. But Amin heard it not, for he, o'erwrought, Had perished in his hour of evil pride.
H. Rosa.

In a village not many miles from Edinburgh lived two worthies named Sandy M'Tavish and John Bain. They were one night sitting in the public-house enjoying a glass of the real Glenlivet, when the talk turned on politics, on which subject they " agreed to differ." The discussion got somewhat heafed, and Sandy, after much eloquent abuse of the statesman from whose policy he differed, thumped the table till the glasses rattled and shouted triumphantly, "I tell ye, John Bain, that ye canna argue awa' facts. Facts are obstinate things." Sandy," was the canny reply, "what a great feet ye maun be " Fatesres.—Amang the oye of girlhood is friend- aWp, which, though often laughed at as absurd and 'Wmish," is, nevertheless, very sweet. Most girls, even if they have sisters, have also some special friend to N'4l6 0. they vow eternal devotion, write voluminous : when they are apart, and for whom they contrive al sorts of little presents, more or less useful or orna- inesetal. If the friend is an ordinarily good girl, this affection is beneficial to both parties, takes each a little out of her own small circle as well as out of herself, and widens her horizon. It is often very pure and unselfish, and, especially between girls who never marry, endures as long as they live.—Front Cassell's Family Magazine" let December. A FAMILY DOCTOR ON SLEEPLESSNRSS.—Think and consider whether of late you have given *ay to any table indiscretion that may have affected the liver, and _ .

rendered it either sluggish or too active. In these cases the.blood will in reality have become poisoned and con- taminated with bile, the mind becomes dull and pro- bably gloomy all day, and over-active towards nightfall. The sure indication of treatment is to strictly regulate the diet for a few weeks, to take an occasional blue pill at night, with a glass of Pullna water half an hour be- fore breakfast, and to take a course of Turkish baths (if permitted by your own medical adviser), with a reason- able amount of exercise in the open air. Dyspepsia will produce sleeplessness, and may in ordinary cases he eured in the same way, though aperients should rather le avoided. Most careful regulation of diet is, however, a Jim pal non. It is not a good plan to go to bed with an entirely empty stomach. Acrain, if the body feels hot, a cold bath, followed by a bottle of soda-water and 15 grains of the bicarbonate of soda, will have a good effect. Sometimes a hot bath will do more good than a cold one; the state of one's own feelings is to be consulted, and results made a mental note of. Do you smoke much? If so, a return to health is not to be expected until the habit is overcome. Exercise in abundance taken during the day in the open air is in hundreds of case- a cure for sleeplessness; but this exercise should not be of a too fatiguing kind—it should be spread over a great many hours, it should be pleasant, calming exercise, and not continued up to a late hour. Over-fatigue must be care- fully avoided. The practice of taking stimulants to any extent is very apt to produce sleeplessness by keeping up an unnatural excitement of the brain. Wine negus has been recommended as a night-cap, and even stronger stimulants. They should only be prescribed by a medical man, for they are narcotics, and narcotics in any form tend to make matters worse in the long run.—Froin " Cassell's Family Mergacine" for December. CHRISTMAS AND OTHER BOOKS. " Peter Parley's Annual" (published by Mr. Be* George, London) has for more than a generation made the mouths of boys and girls water. To sce it is to love it tiA it presents itself in gorgeous binding of scarlet and blue and gold. And it is just as bright inside as colt; for although this is tbe forty-sixth year of pub-. liontion age cannot stale nor custom wither the finite valiety of the stories,. The following are the titles of the tales arid sketches of the annual for 1887 : R ,bert Lind-ay's Inheritance, Catherine and her Fate, Ned Joyce's Atonement, Rise and Progress of Bank- ow, John Edbrook's Birthdays, How Davey got his Blue, Strange Adventures in India, Coal, Gun Gos- sip, and A Modern Castor and Pollux. There are, as iraial, about a score of coloured illustrations—for "Peter Parley" is not Content with black and white —and paper and printitig match in being first-class The annual is a sort of king amongst Christmas ~ shall We Know Them Again P" is the title of a new hook recently published by Messrs. J.Nisbet and Co., L aidee, It is of special interest, in that it is written by a local author (whose name is nit, how- ever, disclosed), wite tho charitable obje(t of aiding a deserving family. The work is" dedicated with all Christian sympathy to Mrs. Fraser, whose noble hus- band (the late Lord Bishop of Manchester) passed away Ootober 22, 1885." Reference is made, by way of illustrating the views of the writer, to the lab. Bishop, to the late John Brooks the first M.P. for the Altriuchana Division, and to the saintly character of too • much loved children, the interest being height- eued by fieely-ioiela d full-page portraits of these worthies. The writer is evidently actuated by a strong feeling of piety, 44 argues with much earnestness that those who p 558 away are "not dead but gone be- fore," and will be known to each othe. • ; better land a . The volutt", it should be mentioned, is beauti- fully printed and handsomely bound. It is to be hoped it will have a large circulaticn. so that the benevolent object. with which it has been issued will be fully achieved.

The full-page illustrations, en tuned Paper, enhance the interest of the stories, and aii much to the appearance of the number. 411,cdotes about Lawyers, Doctors, and Par- song,'' II Mr. John Ti:nbg, is in the nick of time for Christmas reading. It is published by Messr. Dip- rose and Bateman, London, in a handy form and is neatly bound. As might he expected, the anecdotes are 6f the raciest kind, and range from grave to gay from lively to Revere." It is a matter of course t• say that Rowe of the stories are not new. The new- ness and the value of' the book is in their being brought together in this permanent form. Awful Storie,," by the author of "The Stock- broker, Wife" is another publication by Messrs. Di- Prose and Bateman. The stories present themselves " Particularly modern, as they all turn on telephone Secrets. The author is not one to beat about the ,bush ; there an electric touch in all hie work ,• and as ne is neither stab', flat, nor unprofitable, he will have Piety of readers. Another interesting and useful work from the same press relates to "Mistaken Identities.' It far— niches details of the more celebrated cases of impos- tnre, old and new, end the record goes to prove the truth of the saying' that truth is stranger than fiction. The compilation has been well executed by Mr. J. Redding Care,

" The' Poetical Works of Lord Byron," in two volumes, at one shilling each, constitute the cur- rent issue of the Cauterbury Poets, published by Mr. Walter Scott, London. There is an introductory, notice by Mathilde Blind which, based as it is upon the latest-known facts as to Byron's career, is es- pecially interesting. The first volume embraces the miscellaneous poems of the poet, and the second is de- voted to "Childs Harold" and "Don Juan." We have before bad occasion to speak in praise of the binding, paper, and type of this cheap and yet elegant edition of the poets. In the ‘. Camelot Clissics " series, also published by Mr. Walter Scott, the latest issue is ashilling volume bound in the usual red cloth, on "Great English Painters." The work is arranged and edited by Mr. William Sharp, who supplies an instructive introduc- tion. The volume gives an account of the lives of William Ilogarth, Richard Wilson, Sir Joshua Rey- nold, Thos. Gainshorough, and William Blake, and will be welcome alike to the art student and to the general reader.

ta,nt part of the garden where the rhubarb might be I situated, and after it is no longer required it must be wheeled somewhere else, most probably to where it was mixed. The directions given by the writer in question involved all the above labour. Now, as we do not wish our readers to be dragged through this old-fashioned rut, we commend to their notice the following plan, which we have advocated and partly explained in this column. Instead of conveying the heating material to the roots, we take these to the heat, and so reverse matters. Many amateurs and cot- tagers do this, and place them in cellars or under the greenhouse stages, but the result is disappointing in the early part of the year, and in some instances we have known the roots refuse to start at all. If in any corner most convenient for the manure a bed is made about a yard wide, two feet high, and the required length, and the roots lifted and closely packed on that, then covered over with soil or decayed manure, and tubs and more long manure placed over them to keep the heat in, rhubarb forcing becomes safe and simple. If the boxes are not of sufficient depth to allow head room for the rhubarb, the sides of the bed should be carried up to the level of the crowns, so that the boxes will be raised also. Should there be no heat in the bed in a few days, pack some fresh manure round the sides and ends to the height of the bed. A trial stick should be inserted in the bed, and if it feels lukewarm when taken out for ex- amination matters are all right, but if warmer draw the lining away a little from the sides for a day or two. As to tubs, we have made use of cement tubs sawn in two. Farmers might turn many a sweet shilling out of the wasted heat of their muck heap, if they only grew rhubarb and forced it as directed.

The Clydesdale' Association of Canada has issued the first volume of the stud-book. It gives the pedigrees of 1,277 horses and mares. Sir John Errington, Bart., has remitted to his tenantry on the Puddington estate, Cheshire, 10 per cent. on their rents. Mr. Bromley-Devonport, M.P., has also granted 10 per cent. reduction to his tenantry on the Calveley Hall estate. The allotment system has been introduced on an ex- tensive scale on the Linton estates in Kent by Mr. F. S. Cornwallis. Each allotment is to be 20 rods in extent, and will be let at a yearly rental of 55., free of tithes and rates; no person to have more than two allotments. A large number of labourers have already made applica- tion for allotments. The number of Clydesdales sold this year for exporta- tion has been considerably increased of late. Mr. Cars- well, from Kansas, has just shipped nine head. Mr. Wm. Crawford, Bowertrapping, Dairy, has sold to Mr. Arthur ' Watson, Fulwood, Renfrewshire, at a high figure, the promising filly foal, winner in the large class of foals at Ardrossan a few weeks ago. PURE-BRED PIGS IN IRELAND.—The advantages of using pure-bred pigs for breeding purposes have lately been strikingly illustrated in County Down, Ireland. A gentleman residing in that district, who has for a long time been an extensive breeder of swine, introduced into his herd early in the year a few pure-bred animals, and the result has exceeded his highest anticipations. Indeed, so great is his satisfaction that he intends purchasing more during the coming spring, and doing away with all his Irish sows. As he very truthfully remarks, "there is nothing like the pure breed. There are," he goes on to say, "a great number of what we call, the old Irish breed' in this neighbourhood, and I have been struck with the wonderful improvement in the pigs by going to a pure-bred bog. One boar, in particular, has got some marvellous results; in fact, I can hardly keep the people away, running every day with a lot of old sows to him." Thu ENSILAGII SOCIETY.—In the annual competition of this society now being held in London there are 145 samples of ensilage in the ten classes, including speci- mens made from almost all descriptions of fodder. These have been judged with the result that the champion cup was awarded to Mr. C. G. Johnson, the winner of the prize for stack silage in the recent competition of the Royal Agricultural Society. Mr. R. Soder was first out of 47 entries in the meadow grass class, Mr. E. T. Blunt winning in the next class for meadow grass ensi- lage made in a stack, the sample sh ti f

THE GREENHOUSE.-.—III damp weather keep a watch on the plants, and as soon as there are signs of premature decay in flowers or foliage, light a fire early in the morn- ing, and, at the same time, open tee ventilators to allow the moisture to escape; or if on entering a house in the morning the floor and pots look damp, the fire may be .lighted, but it should be let out again before closing up the house for the night. In mild weather 40 to 45 de- grees is a comfortable temperature for most fteenhouse plants, but during frost it should not exceed 40 degrees for any lengthened period. Plants require looking over daily as to water in frosty weather, because the heating apparatus wiU have the effect of drying up the soil in the pots. Ferns and other moisture-loving plants should be as far from the influence of the apparatus as possible.

When wi got to th' station, I tuk care to remember wot hoo towd me and wi got in to a snug carridge, an' as luck would have it, Wi had id aw to eawrsels. It wur splendid to sit deawn on th' soft-cushioned seats, fur wi wur booath van_ ry tired with eawr afternoon's tramp. I wur just gooin t' sleep when th' train stopped an' two swells geet in, booath ov 'em smokin' cigars. Yea should hay' seen th' twinkle in Ann Jane's eye as hoe sed, "Allow me, gentlemen, to inform yoa this is not a smokin' compartment, and I strongly objeckt." Ann Jane popped her yead thro' th' window, air' sheawted eawt at the top of her voice, "Guard! Guard!! Guard!! ! No matter how long Mrs. Ila,rcourt lives, she will never forget that night alone in the great Lonrlon hotel. The very quiet of the carpeted corridors seemed to drive her mad, the comfortable house appeared to mock her; and when she had dismissed her maid and sunk back upon er pillow, the dreams and thoughts that passed before , her waking eyes seemed literally to madden her. Never before had she valued her quiet even life, never before had she realised her love for Brian Verularn ; and as her whole soul revolted at the idea of being once more 1 in the clutches of her husband, she had need of all her strong sense of duty to enable her to remain and greet him, who was as false to her, she felt really, as ever shb had been to him in imagination. At last she determined to allow her future to depend entirely on how he greeted her; if he had any affection for her left she would, as a penance for her wandering thoughts, stay by him, and endeavour to,win him back again, to be true and loyal after all. She had left him to temptation, and men were feeble creatures at best. Mrs. Harcourt stretched out her hand for her Prayer- book, and looked through the vows she had breathed so carelessly on her marriage morning. There was no doubt about them—not the smallest doubt. She must keep them, or be forsworn; keep them, yes. If her hus- band showed he meant to love and: cherish her, she would do her part; she would obey, cherish, and nurse ' ' him to the best of her ability. She had wronged him by ' : marrying him in a fit of pique with Brian, if only he still loved her; she would try and love him in time. Men were so silly, she thought, they could not be content with one love; it was not in their nature to be faithful to a wife so many, many thousand miles away. The night passed; breakfast and luncheon were des- patched ; the discreet waiters asked for orders for dinner, for the maid had whispered to them Mrs. Harcourt's story, and were told none could be given until the Colonel came. The afternoon began to darken, and, bitterly re- sentful of this neglect, Mrs. Harcourt had put on her bonnet, meaning to return home forthwith, when looking for the last time out of the window, she saw a hansom approaching, with her husband inside. I A, Ali! she should hardly have known him, had she not recognised his voice yesterday; and wonderinc, feebly if she were equally altered, she walked to the door, and . opened it just as the Colonel came up the staircase. i For one moment they looked at each other, speechless, ' and then the Colonel, coming forward, held out his hand. ,6 Ah, Lucy," he said, after a pause, "ten years older, I I see;" and then adding. as he entered the sitting-roorn, "I ' hope you have ordered a room for me," he sauntered to the window, and looked carelessly out into the rapidly ' darkening street. Mrs. Harcourt gazed at him for a moment fixedly, and , in that moment made up her mind to her future course. 1 "I will see about your room," she said quite quietly; ! and going out into the passage, she closed the door gently, ' and, without a moment's pause, stepped down the wide staircase, and was speedily en route for the Manor as fast as a hansom, and express train to follow, could take her. ' The next time Colonel Harcourt saw his wife was in the Divorce Court, where he had the pleasure of listening to as long and complete a list of misdemeanours as ever landed a gentleman in that unpleasant locality; while he was obliged to confess that if the ten years had robbed Lucy of much of her youthful grace and beauty, they had given her a great deal in exchange, and that he had lost more than he calculated upon when he so carelessly greeted the graceful, handsome woman who after all, was his wife, and had evidently meant to do her duty by him up to the last moment. He did not alter this opinion when, after some years,' he saw her at Cannes, and contrasted her calm face with the sharp anxious-eyed countenance of his companion, to whom he had allied himself in India, trusting to the obscurity of the up-country station, and the half-intoxi- cated state of the army chaplain who performed the ceremony, for that secrecy which vanished into thin air under the searching light of the Divorce Court; and to which was due the fact that Mrs. Harcourt obtained her freedom, and liberty to marry her old love, in whose company she looked all an English lady should, the while she smiled on their two tiny children, who were lovely and charming enough to command the ad- miration and homage of the whole of the frivolous place, where they were hoping to spend the winter.

"Oh," he groaned, "I've swallowed it." "Well, for good- ness' sake," whispered his wife, "keep quiet, or you'll wake the baby." An old Highlander was ordered by his doctor not to exceed two ounces of spirits daily. He asked how much liquor that was. "Sixteen drams," was the reply. "What a guid doctor," said the Highlander to his son. "Run and tell Donald Me.Davish and Big John to come doon the nicht."

AN AGED OYSTER.—An American eating-house keeper advertised for "a boy to open oysters fifteen years old." When an oyster becomes such a veteran, its age should be kept a secret, the same as a spring chicken's. Surely an oyster ought to be able to open itself long before it reaches its fifteenth year. Lawyer: "You say you made an examination of the premises. What did you find?" Witness: "Oh, nothing of consequence--a 'a beggarly account.of empty bones,' as Shakspere says!" Lawyer: "Never mind what Shakspere said. He will be summoned and testify for himself, if he knows anything about the case." The art of receiving and entertaining agreeably and gracefully is possessed in perfection only by the woman of tact, and it is sometimes said that small dinner parties are the test of a woman's social abilities. A crowd will take care of itself; but the smaller circle depends very much more upon the capabilities of its hostess. IRISH BOARD OF GUARDIANS DISSOLVRD. - The New Ross Board of Guirdians recently opened a "ward of hon- our " in the workhouse for the reception of evicted tenants, and allowed them an extraordinary diet and other privi. ieges at the public expense. The Irish Local Govern- ment Board remonstrated, and, being defied," has die. soived the Board of Guardians and appointed paid officials to talc.-, charge of the affairs of the union.

div.p: COTTA GE GARDENING.

On Wednesday and Thursday mornings, the Ist and 2nd, from 10 to 13 degrees of frost were registered in many gardens, and the surface of the soil was bound cement like and rendered valuable assistance in the per- formance of certain operations that we did not care to commence upon with a sloppy soil underfoot. Wheeling manure on a frosty morning, when the ground is hard, is not an unpleasant task, and later in the day pruning fruit trees is equally agreeable. In addition to wheeling manure on vacant spaces, we deposited some also be- tween the celery trenches, and spread it, having pre- viously forked the ground to the subsoil, and when the celery comes to be dug the soil will be levelled and the ground will then be in good order for either peas or onions, or any other crop requiring good tilth. If much celery is grown in a garden, and the above practice followed, there will be no need for trenching, as with the trenches made for celery planting and the forking be- tween the rows the ground gets well distributed, and as no crop pays better and prepares the soil for other crops so well as celery, its culture might with advantage be extended in many gardens. The frost, for the time it lasted, revolutionised our doings in other ways, and for the first time since spring we had to look sharp in all directions fcr protective materials for cauliflowers, lettuce, and other tender plants. Parsley we cover, in case of snow falling and making it difficult to pick. Beetroot had to be hastily taken up. They have been exposed to as much frost as is good for them, and those who have not taken up the roots should do so at once. Take every care not to injure the roots, for loss of colour will be the result of their being broken or lacerated. Trim the leaves to within three or four inches of the bot- tom, and then pack the roots on their sides, with the crown outward, in soil, sand, or ashes, and out of the reach of frost. Parsnips are best in the ground, but as this sometimes becomes frozen so hard that the assist- ance of a pickaxe is required to release anything in it, a few roots should be taken up and covered with ashes, which soon give way to the fork or spade even in very sharp frost. Carrots are more tender, and the whole crop is usually taken up and treated similarly to beet- root. Turnips keep quite fresh if taken up pd " clumped " similar to potatoes, and as they get bruised when taken up in frosty weather it would be as well to treat all the forward roots in this way, and as they do not withstand the severest winters the bulk of the crop will be secured. It is regarded a feat to have rhubarb ready by Christmas, and more gardeners fail in produc- ing it than succeed. A writer in one of the gardening papers recently laboured to explain and advocate the antiquated and cumbrous method of forc- ing it that we have been long acquainted with. There would not be quite so much fault to find with the writer for repeating these instructions if the carrying of them out affected the object desired. Un- fortunately this is not the case, and the rhubarb is just as .likely to be three months as one before it is fit for use, and it would be nothing unusual to learn that the crowns had been scalded and the crop destroyed for the year. Readers of garden literature may have seen in old books on the subject that in order to force rhubarb it was necessary to have sundry cartloads of manure and leaves !nixed together, and turned over two or three times, at intervals of a week. Then it is fit for use, and after the roots are covered with pots or boxes abe of it several feet wide—in some instances yards—and not less than a yard deep was recommended to cover the whole. But that is only part ot the labour. As the work of preparing the material could not be very well conducted in a garden it must take place somewhere outside it. TURKEY.—RUSSIA'S ATTITUDE. The Bulgarian Government has sent an envoy.to Con- stantinople to induce the Porte to pat forward a more ac- ceptable candidate for the Bulgarian throne than the Prince of Mingrelia. CONSTANTINOPLE, SIINDLY.—It is declared in eTplonnetio circles that the object of Russia is to prevent the rorte from pink: the Western Powers, rod to wait for a revolution. ary movement in Bulgaria to afford her an opportunity to intervene. • VIENNA, MoN-Day.—A. despatch from Sefie states that on Saturday Gadb&n Effendi presented to the Regents a t4yr lrizieriel Note, demending, in the name of hie mejesty the Sultan, V.-let the Bulgarians should receive the Prince 0 litingrelia before it is too late. The Regents and elinisters* adhere to their intention ef holding no further' Personal in. tercourse with the Turkish Ambassador. SEVEN HUNDRED DACOITS SURPRISED. MANDALAY, WEDNESDAY.—A. considerable BuccesS was- gainea against the dacoits on Saturday. Colonel -Heyland, with fifty lancers of the Myingyar Brigade, surprised even hundred dacoite, and pursued them over the country, which was favourable to cavalry. He killed two hundred of them and captured three Bobs and a quantity of arms and am- munition. Colonel Heyland and one lancer were elightlY woundcd. At Isfyinmoo. on the 10th, Lieutenant Rolland, when pursuing • lila On, captured his camp, his wife, a large quantity of ammunition, and two of Ilia Ws lieu- tenants, who surrendered. nine jungle camps were covered.

GERMANY'S POLICY OF PEACE. The German Minister of War, at Monday's sitting a elle Military Committees to discuss the bill providing for the increase of the army, said if Princo Bismarck himself had been present he would have. added nothing to what had already been officially stated- as to the necessity for adding to the effective strength of the army, seeing that a more detailed statement as to the intimate rerations between individual Powers and their possible policy could mot be made known without rendering Germany's policy of peace more difficult of accomplishment. The committee der aided to allow the bill to be read a first and second time,and than to enter upon the discussion of the clauses. The armament of the German army with a repeating rifle is now being carried out with all haste. The new weapon is already in the hands of a company of the 2nd Foot Gnards, which formed the guard of honour to the Prince Regent of Bavaria, FRANCE.—TIIE NEW PREMIFR AND CABINET. M. Goblet. the new Premigr, made a Ministerial state- ment in the French Chamber of Deputies on Saturday, which was well received. He said that in foreign policy he would follow the line marked out by the preceding Cabinet and approved by the Chamber. THE BURMAII CAMPAIGN. Six strong detachments of Anglo-Indian troops will start to surround the position held by the Burmese insurgent leader Boshway. DAMAGING THE " DOUBLE-B ASS."

The services of the Gospel mission in the Co- operative Hall, Earlestown, were on Sunday evening last attended by a singular accident. Shortly after the conclusion of the service, the preacher had oc- casion to speak to Mr. Birks, one of the leaders of the mission. Mr. Birks, in turning round, acciden- tally placed his foot upon a large double-bass fiddle, which is used with other stringed instruments as an accompaniment to the singing. The instrument was not a little damaged, the strings and frame- work'being smashed. It was the property of Mr. Warden, of Legh-street, and was worth several pounds.
Hi diddle, diddle, A tale of a fiddle— Mr. Birks, now what have you done? Oh it's you, and you've put your foot in it too, And so there's an end of the fun.
Dear-a-me, Mr. Warden, You should have been guarding That fiddle of your's, but, alas, You let Birk's big toe run against it, and 80 There's an end of the great double bass.
WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART. THE ANNUAL MEETING.

On Monday the annual meeting of the subscribers to the Warrington School of Art was held at the School. Mr. John Rylands presided, and there were als present Messrs. John Dun, E. Brewtnall, Fred. Monks, Thomas Birtles, H. N. Houghton, John Hatton, Robert Garnett, William Owen (hon. trea- surer and secretary), and H. D. Barkas (head master).
THE RE&D MASTER'S REPORT.

Mr. BARKAS read his annual report, which contained the following items :—I am pleased to inform You that during the past session the work of the school has continued to make satisfactory progress. The large number of prizes and certificates awarded to this school by the Examiners of the Science and Art Department is an eviience of the continued industry and ability on the part of the students. The num- ber of students under instruction during the past session was 235, showing an increase of 11 over the number en- tered on the school-books during the previous year. The figures stand thus : Science, 30 students; Art, 205 students. Ninety-nine students attended the day classes and paid the higher fee ; whilst 137 were registered as attending the evening classes only, almost the whole of the latter being artizens, mechanics, and pupil teachers. By this it will be seen that the advantages offered to the evening classes to working people are appreciated, and the important object of the school is being fulfilled. In April upwards of 3,500 drawings and paintings were submitted to the examiders to compete for marks, certificates, and prizes, the result being 17 third grade prizes were awarded for works in advanced stages. These prize drawings on being forwarded for still higher awards in the national competition resulted in Mr. Hollins Allen receiving a gold medal for a set of three de- signs for stair carpets. This is the highest award at the disposal of the Department. A Society of Arts bronze medal (Owen Jones memorial prize) was also awarded the same student for the same drawings. I would here stare that out of 227 Schools of Art in the •United Kingdom, 11 received 12 gold medals, Nyarrinton receiving one. The results of the examinations bonducted in May are satisfac- tory. The requisite drawings and examinations being satisfactorily completed, `1 art class teachers' certificates " have been awarded to Miss Mary Burgess, Miss Annie Guest Downe, and Mr. Hollins Allen. The members of the Vacation Sketching Club have again done good work. The drawings and paintings brought together in October last to compete for prizes showed considerable advance on last year. In conclusion Mr. Barkas said: I have now to express to you my appreciation of the services of my assis- tant teachers, Miss Mary Burgess, Miss Annie Chrimes. and Mr. Hollins Allen. To Mr. C. B. Aylward, my assis- tant master. lam indebted for his valuable aid. Both in science and art his (Mr. Aylward's) teaching has proved most effective. Last, but not least, allow me to offer my thanks to Mr. Wilbato Owen for his untiring exertions on behalf of the school and his unvarying kindness to masters and students. The report was adopted, on the motion of Mr.l.Dter, se- corded by Mr. HOUGHTON.
STATE ,TENT OF ACCOUNTS

Mr. OWEN then read the following statement of accounts, which was adopted, for tbe session from September Ist, 1886, to July 4th, 1886 :—School fees, £396 163 63 ; sub- scriptions, £43 14193 ; Government grant, £204 17s 9.1; transferred from reserve fund, £10; department, £lO •, in- terest, 43; to deficit, £46 83 43 ; total. £7ll 17s Bd. Deficit balance, £35 23; salaries for teaching, die., £372 3.3 41; printing, advertising, &c., £lB lie; gas and wAter. £43 193; coal and slack, £ll 4s 81; new casts, £2 15s 9.1: insurance, £2 143; cheque book, 6; 3d; Mr. 13.3rkas (grant), £ll4 183 83; Mr. Aylward, do., £57 93 4.1: J. C. Thompson, do., 41 103; sundries, £5O 4a 51; bank commission, 163 10.1; bank interest. 23 5.1; total, £7ll 173 Bd. Mr. Owen added that, though the deficit appear( d larger than et the end of the previous session, it really was not so, as the outstanding li- abilities at the end of the session 1834-5 were £79 123 93, whereas at the end of the session 1835-6 they ware only £63 23 43. Thelast session showed an advantage of £l6 103 6.1 over the previous one.

PROPOSED EXTENSION OP THE SCHOOL. The CHAIRMAN called attention to the fact that the school was already tOOO small, and he added that they should be glad if they could see their way to increase it. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. BriEverNaLL said they wanted a model- ling room, and also a designing room. He added that ladies who came from outside towns did not know what to do with themselves during the middle of the day, and if they had a small luncheon-room, where a cup of tea and other suitable refreshments might be obtained, he was persuaded it would considerably help a number of 'outside students. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Dux suggested that Mr. Owen should make a sketch plan of the additional accommodation required, and if the committee would approve of a report to be drawn up showing what had been done in the school, and what could be done if they had greater accommodatiop, it might be put before half a dozen people who took an interest in the school and•district with some chance of making the exten- sion and of clearing oft the existing debt. —The CHAIRMA.N There is no doubt that the school has progressed more rapidly than we anticipatel—The subject then dropped.

GOOD TEmPLABT.—The Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars held its session on Monday evening in the Lodge Room, Bridge-street, Earlestown, when Brother John Taylor, W.C.T., presided. There was a good attend- ance, and after . the opening proceedings four new candi- dates were admitted to membership. Arrangements were made for plying a fraternal visit to the Ashton Lodge. The evening's programme was "Sale of varieties," and a selec- tion of miscellaneous articles were presented by the members for disposal. The W.C.T. officiated as" auctioneer," and a fair sum was realised in aid of the funds of the Lodge. Tun COMB CAMPBELL CASE.—On Saturday the sitting of the Divorce Court was entirely taken up with the cross- examination and re-examination of Lady Colin Campbell. On Monday Mrs Blood, the mother of Lady Colin, gave evi- dence. She stated that her daughter's acquantance with the Duke of Marlborough had her approval. She considered the Duke to be "not a bit worse than other men," and " a fitting companion for a beautiful young married woman." Mr. Justice Butt intimated that if he sat till twelve o'clock every night he would conclude the case before the holidays. —ln the Campbell ease on Wednesday the Duke of Marl- borough was examined as a witness in his own defence. He denied the charge made against him. It may be remembered that one of the main allegations against Lady Cdlin was that she had spent two days with the Duke at Purfleet. In his opening statement on bsbalf of the duke the Attorney- General denied, with great emphasis, that the duke was ac- companied by a lady on the occasion of his visit to Purfket. In making that statement the Attorney-General of course acted on" instructions" since confirmed by the duke at a personal interview. But in the witness-box on Wednesday the duke, knowing what the consequences might be if he asserted on oath that be was " alone," admitted that he went to Purfleet with a " lady "—not Lady Colin, but a woman of low character. He had lied to his solicitors and his coun- sel because be thought an admission of the truth might be injurious to his character. His meetings with Lady Colin in Paris and the story of his divorce were also the subject of cross-examination. Captain Shaw denied on oath the charge brought against him, and the Court adjourned. On Thurs- day the hearing of evidence in this case was concluded, and counsel delivered their " summing up " addresses to the jury. Some sensation was created in court by the announce- ment that Colonel Butler, who is one of the co-respondents, was not to be salted as a witness. The Colonel's counsel asked that the case against him might be withdrawn by the Judge, but Mr. Justice Butt declined, and remarked that there was evidence to go to the jury. • MONST, MONET, MONEY.—Loans of money advanced at the lowest rate of interest.—Apply at 7, Wellington- street, Earlestown. All business strictly confidential. Advt.

-- - TWENTY-SEVEN LIVES LOST. The total number of lives lost threiugh the cap- sizing of the Southport and St. Anne's lifeboats is twenty-seven, fourteen from the former boat and thirteen from the latter. • MESSAGE FROM THE QUEEN. Telegrams have been received from General Pon- sonby, on behalf of the Queen, and the secr4ary to the Lifeboat Institution. The Queen exprestes her sympathy with the relatives of the lifeboat men who were drowned while heroically attempting to save life during the recent gale, and her tender message has been deeply appreciated. OPENING OF THE INQUEST.

The inquest on the bodies of the men who were drowned through the capsizing of the Southport and. St. Anne's lifeboats, and whose bodies had been re- covered, was opened at the Palace Hotel, Birkdale, on Saturday, by Mr. Samuel Brighouse, county coroner. Twenty-five of the bodies had been found 'up to time of the inquest, and two were still miss- ing. The jury proceeded to -view the bodies, twenty-three of which were deposited in the stables adjoining the Palace Hotel. Another body, which was picked up on the shore at an early hour on Saturday morning, was lying in the Victoria Hotel. The other body was that of John Ball, a member of the Southport crew, who died in the infirmary late on Friday night firm the effect of the injuries which he received through the *sizing of the lifeboat. When the jury returned from viewing the bodies evidence of identification was taken, and the inquest was then formally adjourned until to-day, when it is expected that the inquiry will be completed.

OFFICIAL INQUIRY. The official inquiry into the loss of the South- port and St. Annes lifeboats commenced on Monday I at Southport. Evidende was given by John Jackson and Henry Robinson, the two survivors, as to the cause of the capsizing of the Southport boat. Jackson: said that when the accident happened the anchor, of which he was in charge, was over the side. He thought that the boat ought to have righted in spite of the fact that the anchor was ' hanging over her bows, and he. did not think the i men clinging to the thwarts inside the boat would have hindered her if she had 'made an effort" to right herself. The fact was that she never did try to right herself. Thomas Clarkson, the coxswain of , the Lytham boat, by which the wrecked crew were ; taken from the Mexico, gave a description of the ; rescue; and other evidence having been given of ' the finding of thn bodies and the two boats, the in- quiry was adjourned until Wednesday. The official inquiry was resumed at South- port. On Wednesday Sir Digby Murray read a letter he had received from Blackpool in which it was stated that the coxswain of the St. Alines boat was in the last stage of con- sumption at the time of the disaster, and was therefore two weak to steer the boat. Lieutenant Tipping, the district inspector of the Lifeboat In- stitution, said he had known Johnston, the cox- swain of the St. Annes boat, six or seven years. During that time he had not seen any perceptible change in his appearance. He heard at the begin- ning of November that Johnston had consumption and was not.likely to recover; but after that he saw Johnston, and to all appearances he was in excellent health. The other evidence given related mainly to the state of the tides, the set of the different cur-. rents on the shore, and the different lights that were seen on the night of the storm. The Emperor of Germany has contributed £250 to the fund for the widows and children of the Southport and St. Annes crews. A committee has also been formed to raise a fund at Hamburg, the port to which the Mexico belonged. Subscriptions are pouring in from all parts of England. The bodies of the men drowned by the capsizing of the Southport and St. Annes lifeboats were buried on Tuesday. A public funeral was given to thirteen of them at Southport, and similar ceremonies took place at Lytham and St. Annes'. Sir Digby Murray, from the Board of Trade, and Captain the Hon. 11. W. Chetwynd, Chief Inspector for the Royal National Lifeboat Institution, visited St. Annes and Lytham, on Thursday, for the pur- pose of .examining the lifeboats there, and also of hearing evidence as to the health of Johnson, the coxswain of the St. Annes boat, and the rest of the boat's crew. Dr. Easton, of Lytham, under whose care Johnson had for some time been, said that the man was not actually in the last stage of consump- tion, but he was suffering from that disease. He was quite unfit to go to sea in the boat, and in go- ing out in her he acted against witness's orders, as well as against the rules of the club of which Johnson was a member. The other members of the crew were not a strong set of men; in fact some of them were very weak. The inquiry terminated yesterday.

CO-OPERATION AMONGST FARMERS. Amongst the many devices acrriculturists are just now forced to resort to in order to improve or rather maintain their condition in the face of fall- ing prices, that of association or bo-operation for the purpose of bringing their produce 'directly to the door of the consumer, so to speak, is one of the most important, and the most promising of re- sults. It may have been noticed from an advertise- ment that appeared in our columns last week, that Warrington has become the centre of one of these movements on the part of the farmers of the neigh- bourhood. The large building which directly faces a person who is passing from• Horsemarket-street into,Bewsey-street is to be the local, habitation and business head-quarters of the recently-formed "Lancashire and Cheshire Farmers' Co-operative Association Limited," and it is being rapidly trans- omed by ifessrs. Collin and Sons, under the direc- t.ion of Mr. Beesley, architect, into a place suitable 'or the purposes of the Association. According to the announcement, it is intended to sell on 'these Premises, "butchers' meat, milk, butter, green- grocery, and farm produce of every description," and the whole of these articles it is intended should be supplied by the members of the Association themselves. The Association at the present time, we believe, consists of between fifty and sixty shareholders, who have taken up almost the whole of the four hundred £5 shares, the chairman of the Company being Mr. John White, and the secretary B, Melville. Matters are now so far •ad- vanced that a manager—Mr. William Thompson, %from near Stockoort—has been appointe4, and it is intended to open out the department for the sale of er's meat on Wednesday next. The de- partments for the sale of milk, greengroceries, but- ter, and the various other agricultural products will be °P.eliled in the early part of January. For the home team, Wooley, Barton, Ashton, Blackledge, Dykes, Highley, and Bellian played beat, and McCann was the best for the visitors. WARRINGTON "A " v: HIGRYIELD let TAM.—The above teams appeared at Warrington on Saturday before a good muster of spectators. Warrington had a very inferior team, owing to the first team taking with them several of , their beat forwards. Whittle kicked off for Warrington at 3-15 p.m., a poor 'return being made. A scripmage was formed, from which Whittle got hold and passed to Board- man, who kicked into touch in the Highfield quarters. Cra- ghat], Eves, and Whittle worked the ball near the Highfield line. The visiting forwards, however, took the oval out of danger, Mather kicking into touch. Foster next made a dashing run, being brought down by Bandies. The High- field front rank were prominent, taking play to the Warring- ton 25, where Berry picked up and ran near the goal line, where he was pushed into touch, the visitors shortly after- wards forcing Hewitt to touch down. Whittle dropped out, Berr r returning. Hackett, however, removed the pressure, and ITesworth made a good effort; but Berry replied by panting down the field, Boardman being collared before be could make any return. Hackett and Eyes now made a eantiful dribble. but Pennington kicked into touch. Jones and Adamson were next conspicuous by a neat dribble; but Berry stopped their progress. Whittle now got possession and dashed through his opponents and passed to Craghan, who ran near ibis visitors' line, where a scrimmage was formed, the Warringtonians working the ball over the line, a minor resulting. Unsworth returned the drop oat, the same player shortly after patting in a good dribble, but Berry averted danger by a flying kick. Antrobus was now allowed a free kick for off side play, the ball going into touch in neutral ground. The Warrington men, however, were not to be denied, and rushed the ball over the High- field ' line, where a maul ensued between Craghan, Unsworth, and Gee, the home men gaining posses- sion, but the referee only allowed a minor. Half time was now called, the score standing—Warrington 2 minors to 1 minor. Berry restarted the oval for Highfield, Mather re- turning into tench. Whittle, Eyes, and Jones now showed up well in a splendid dribble, taking the ball half the length of the field and looked like scoring, bat Daniels saved. The visiting forwards relieved, Hewitt having to drop on the ball. From the line out Whittle passed to Boardman, who, nearly got over. A scrimmage was formed, the home front rank taking the sphere over the line, but only a dead ball was registered. The visiters next broke away and kicked to Hewitt, who failed to gather the ball, and Boardman saved near his own line. Antrobus was now very prominent, getting clear away from the scrimmage and patting in a good punt to Daniels, but this player kicked into touch in the centre. Telford, Adamson, Jones, and Unsworth dribbled to the Highfield line, but their efforts were only rewarded with a dead bill. After the drop out Mather got hold and passed to Bandies, who made a good run and kick, Highfield having again to touch down. Shortly after the drop out Eyes secured the bill from the scrimmage, and after a splendid run grounled the oval over the line, but the referee (who could not see the point) dis- allowed the try. Shortly afterwards time was called, the game being left drawn in favour of Warrington, the score 1 being—Warrington "A ".6 minors, Highfield Ist 1 minor. 1 Teams :—Warrington: Full Back, Hewitt; three-quarter backs, Bandies, Mather, poardmah ; half-backs, Antrobus and Whittle (captain); forwards. Unswortb, Craghan, Jones, Adamson, Telford Hackett, Eyes, Holland, Niccisson. Highfield: Fall back, Daniels; three-quarter backs, J. Foster, Pritchford, Cooper; half-backs, T. Berry (captain) and Pennington; forwards, T. Gee, Wilcock, Pickering, C. Foster, W. Foster, G. Daniels, Waterwerth, J. Pritchard, Melling. , WARRINGTON v. NEW BRIGHTON. The return match between these two teams.was played at Liscard, on Saturday, and lthough the Warrington team was made aro of several " A " team men , they managed to win an easy victory. The usual first team men who were ab- sent were the captain (Ashton), and the brothers Turner and- Dillon. . The ground, owing to the severe weather daring the pre- vious day, was in a deplorable condition, accurate passing and running almost being an impossibility. Murdoch won the spin, and chore to play with a slight wind in his fav- our. Nevins and Ashurst prevented Tomlinson from mak- ing a good return to touch. Barnes first showed up by a very nice run to home quarters, Male retaliating by a strong kick. Fine open play now ensued, until Gilbert picked up smartly and got in a short run and kick. Barnes next seemed like scoring, Male stopping his progress in the nick of time. Murdoch now obtained a free kick, which was of no advantage, as the ball fell into the hands of Barnes, who put in a dodgy run and was collared by Murdoch with the oval in its original position, viz., the home 25. Murdoch from a pass by Slater put in a short run, but was speedily brought to grief by Jolley. Gilbert put in a long kick, and and Massey following up, a minor was the result. Barnes now got a free kick, play raging in the home quarter. The ball net coming along with the screw let in the home forwards, but Gilbert was a stumbling block to their pro- gress; and immediately afterwards the same player collared Tomlinson with the ball in his possession in the home 25. Shortly afterwards another minor was registered for the visitors, Ashurst almost getting a try by good following up. New Brighton kicked out, but for off side play a scrimmage was formed at the 25 flag. Very soon the home lines were in jeopardy, Barnes again nearly scoring, but .Murdoch and Male successfully repelled his eff irts ta score. Slater put in a good kick, and Brown following up took the oval for the first time over the visitors' line, to the great delight of the spectators. Play now raged for a short time on the visitors' line, but the home team were not destine a to scare, Speakman playing a grand game on the defensive, and re- moving hostilities to healthier quarters for his side. Mas- sey put in a good kick, and from the scrimmage • Speakman got hold and made a good pass to Barnes after he had ran a short distance, the little centre almost scoring; but he made up for. it afterwards by securing the first try after a dodgy run, Speakman failing to kick the goal. From the kick out Speakman put in a good kick to touch. Barnes next gave Massey a good pass, but the latter player failed to hold. Ashurst, at the end of the line out, now passed in a praiseworthy manner to Barnes, who gained ground. Half time was soon called, with the score Warrington one try . two minors .to nil. Brown re-started, • and Barnes returned. Kicks were next exchanged between Barnes, Murdoch, and Appleton, and Rigby by puzzling play, and by the aid of the visitors' forwards, took the oval to the line. Speakman at this point passed in his peculiar style to Barnes, who was within an ace of dropping a goal. Jolley, however, following the kick up, grounded the oval over the line, and from the place Speakman kicked a fine goal. Barnes returned the kick off, and Gilbert saved a nice rash. Speakman 'now passed to' Jolley, who took the oval to the line. The home forwards, however, returned to the charge, and took play to centre, where Barnes obtained possession, made a dodgy run, and looked all over a scorer, bat preferred to pass to Massey. who galloped round his qpponents and secured the third tre. Ashurst was entrusted with the place, but failed to convert it into a major point. Jolley, from the kick out, made an excellent dribble to 25, and Barnes shortly afterwards made an astonisbing dodgy ran in scoring his second try, Jolley failing at goal.. From the kick out the home team Were quickly put on the defensive, and Nevins, Molyneaux, Davies, Mime, and Speakman took the oval over the line. Speakman had the honour of touching it down, but the try was not allowed. From the scrimmage Gilbert made a tre- mendous rush over, a maul ensuing, the visitors' captain having the best of it, but again Speakman failed to notch the coveted point.. Jolley was next conspicuous by a fine dribble, the same player also saving well. A free kick was next acceded to the home team for off side play. Ashurst again passed to Barnes, who in turn re-passed to Masses", who was well stopped on the line after a long ran by Male. The finest piece of play was witnessed on the home side just at the close of time, Leech, Murdoch. and Male passing grandly, and taking play to visitors' 25 when the referee blew his _whistle and brought an end to a very pleasantly contested and fine open game of 50 minutes, the sore being Warrington 1 goal, 4 tries, 2 minors to nil. The game, in a general way, was a fine *pen game, and very pleasantly contested. From a spectator's point of • view nothing could be better, as packed scrimmages were almost done away with, thereby affording opportunities of running and passing; but owing to the greasy nature of the oval passing was to some extent defective. Just at the present time the Warringtonlans are playing an,excellent i game. their screw scrummaging coming off to perfection. The New Brighton contingent struggled manfully, but the superior force brought against them in the end told, as play almost all the time was in their quarters. For the home team, Male and Murdoch played an excellent defensive game. Brown was always prominent in the ranks of the forwards. For the visitors, Barnes never played a batter game in his life, his 'dodgy runs fairly electrifying the spectators. One pass of his is especially worthy of mention, viz.,' when he got the ball near the centre of the field, made a dodgy run to 25, than stopped short and made a long pass to Massey, who easily galloped round his opponents and gained a very meritorious try. His two partners, Jolley and Massey, played with excellent judgment, Jolley especially being noticeable in the tackling department. Gilbert, the captain, played a masterly game quite up to his usual good form, whilst Speakman completely non-plussed his opponents by his peculiar style ef passing. He also played a good defensive game. The-forwards one and all played a good combined game. Davies, Littlewood, and Pevey at times showing up prominently. I Teams :—New Brighton : Back, Tomlinson; three- quarter bachs, Male, Mardoch (captain), and Rigg ; half- backs, Leech and Slater ; forwards, Brawn, A Williams, S Williams, J H Williams, Dodd, Manifold, Gifford, and Muir. Warrington : Back, Appleton; three-quarter backs, Jolley, Barnes, and Massey; half-backs, Gilbert (captain) and Speskman; forwards, 'nein& Rigby, Povey, Davies, Littlewood, Ashurst. Molyneanx. Hough. and, Jiayes. Re: terse, Mr. Parry, secretary of W.L.B.T.R.U. • NOTES BY THE WAY.

The game at New Brighton was a rather one-sided affair' but a very pleasant one, and it is to be hoped that War- rington will have a fixture with them next season. From what we can learn that popular player Tommy Barnes intends to join a stronger club than the Warrington Foot- ball Club, and I am sure he has the good wishes of hundreds of his admirers in this his new undertaking: W. Dillon is again down to play on Saturday, but the popular Wartington captain and. Fair Turner are still suf- fering. Askam-in-Farness come down to-day with a strong team. It will be remembered that this noted club beat the cup holders when en their tour in the Furness district. A good game should therefore be'the result of the encounter ' The game on Saturday was one in which the backs took

lan active part, all scoring with the exception of the fall back, but Speakman's try was not allowed. Broughton visited Liverpool with a weak team on Satru. day, and sustained a defeat at the bands of the Liverpool Old Boys to the tune of one goal, one try, and five minors to four minors. Liverpool also scored in the match with Broughton Rangers, having registered at the close one goal, two tries, and five minors to one minor. The match between Salford and Hull drew together a large concourse of specta- tcrs on the ground of the latt,-r club. Salford were, how- ever, without five of their regular team, and the result was a victory for Hull by three tries to one. Swinton have added to their laurels by their defeat of Swansea, by one goal and two tries to one try.
GENERAL NEWS.

Judgment was given at York, on Saturday, in the Buck- rose election petition. The court found that Mr. Sykes had been duly elected by a majority of 11 votes. MORE JUBILEE MUNIFICENCE.—At a meeting of the Council of University College, Dundee, on Monday, it was announced that Mr. Thcmas H. Cox, of Cox Brothers, jute spinners, had given £l2OOO to endow and equip a chair of anatomy in the medical school it is proposed to establish. Judge Boyd announced in the Land Court on Monday that to adopt "the plan of campaign "in respect of any estate before that Court would be clearly am act of " con- tempt," and said he should know how to deal with both the persons who paid the money and the persons who re- ceived it. DEATH FROM EXTOFUHE ON 1 WELSH MOI7NTAIN.—A woman named Elizabeth Richards, aged 66, residing at Twyncsrno, crossed the mountain during the storm to Trede- gar to seek relief from the guardians, and co returning home she was blown out of the path and perished on the moun- tain near Cern Golan.

For all kinds of domestic sewing, Bagley and Wright's cotton Is the best.—Aelet. MR. CHAMBERLAIN AT HOME.-Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, accompanied by Mr. Jesse Collings, Mr. Richard Chamber- lain, and Mr. Austin Chamberlain, arrived at Birmingham on Tuesday from London. Mr. Chamberlain, who looked wonderfully well, at once proceeded to Highbury. There was no demonstration at the railway station. A BOY CHOKID WITH A PENCIL-HOLDER.—An inquest was held on Saturday evening at Newtown, North Wales, on the body of John Francis Morgan, aged nine, son of a local flannel merchant. The deceased accidentally swal- lowed the top joint of a penny metallic pencil-holder, which lodged in the windpipe, and he died before medical aid arrived.

A MOTHER AND THREE CHILDREN BURNT TO DEATH.— A fire broke out at a grocer's shop at Sutton, Surrey, on Tuesday morning, during which a woman and three of her children were burnt to death before they could be rescued. Anotber child was severely burnt, and had to be removed to the Croyden Hospital. A second woman who was in the house, and the husband of the deceased escaped uninjured. In their report for the year ending the 21st Angust, the Irish Land Commissioners state that the number of fair rents determined was 3,917, and the average reduction was 24 1 per cent. Under Lord Ashbonrne's Act 2,426 leans, to the amount of £1,065,444, :were provisionally sanctioned. The average price paid was 16 years' purchase, at which figure 1,204 conveyances to tenants were passed during the year. An enthusiastic demonstration of the tenantry of the Kingston estate, who accepted the "plan of campaign," was held on Monday at Mitchelstown. Mr. J. O'Connor, M.P., told the tenantry now was the time to strike the blow, as the rents of the future would be fixed in proportion to the rents now paid. By that stroke the Kingston tenantry would add £l,OOO to their capital. Strong resolutions were adopted. THE ECCLESIASTICAL COMMISSIONERS DTSTRAINING FOR TITHES.—Ihs bailiffa arrived at Whitford, Flint, from Lon- don on Tuesday, and, on behalf of the Ecclesiastical Com- missioners, distrained upon five farmers for nonpayment of tithe rent charges due last July. All the defendants are members of the Anti-Tithe Defence League, and their cases have been taken in band by that body. Popular feeling is very excited. Public Analysts have submitted CADBURY'S COCOA to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing beverage. Beware of Imitations. A dot. At Munster Assizes, held at :Cork. on Monday, six young men of the farming class were indicted en the charge of raiding on the house of Abraham Huggard, solicitor, Kil- lorglin, Kerry, at midday on August 11. The defence was an alibi, and after 20 minutes' consultation, the jury ac- quitted Michael Murphy,' one of the prisoners, but could not agree regarding the others. The five remaining prisoners were then put back. THE FASTING MAN IN LONDON.—AlexAndre Jacques, the man who is endeavouring to rival, at Dieudonne's Hotel, St. James's, London, the fasting performance in Paris, had reached the eleventh day of his trial of abstinence on Sat- urday. He takes long walks daily, escorted by one of hisi guardians, arid on Saturday was out for,two hours. His weight, which was 1301 b. on the first day of his fast, was 1231 b. on Saturday. SENTENCES ON SKYE CROFTERS.—ID the High Court of Justiciary, Edinburgh, on Tuesday, Lord More sentenced to three months imprisonment, the six crofters found:grailty.on Monday evening, of mobbing and rioting at Hot neskiraig. on the Kilmnre estate, in Skye, when Sheriff Hamilton and some sheriff's officers were engaged in serving charges for the payment of rent. His lordship observed that had it not been for the jury's recommendation to mercy, he would have pronounced a much heavier sentence. "How TO BE HIPPY, TROUGH MARRIED."—The London correspondent of the "Irish Times," on Monday, says another domeseic romance is being prepared for the London court. The principals are a veteran soldier on the verge Of fourscore and his wife, a young lady of twenty-five, who married twelve months ago. It was stated that on one occa- sion the venerable husband was set upon by his young wife and actually kicked downstairs, and that another time she called for him at his club, and when he came out on the steps, thrashed him with his osi,n walking stick. Mr. Labouchere, ;speaking at Glasgow the other night, alluded to the Crofters' question, and said the landlords had outraged humanity. merely for their m'serable, sordid in- terests. He had read in a sensational divorce case that the Duke of Argyle kept a latch key,and would allow no one else in the house but himself to have a latch key. It seemed this was pretty muds the case with, a good many landlords; because not only did they wish to carry latch keys of their own house, but they wished to turn the key npon the poor people, because they refused to do what landlords wanted.

HYDROPHOBIA FROM THE BITE OF & CAT.—An inquest was held at Manchester. on Friday, on the body of limes Farrell, beer retailer. On the 8:h of August deceased was badly bitten in the thumb by a cat which he was trying to drive out of his cellar. He had often since complained of pain in his arm. On Tuesday week the pain became acute, and he appeared to have spasms whenever he was in a dranght. He was taken to the infirmary, where be died on Thursday. The symptoms were those of hydrophobia, and the jury found that death was due to that disease, caused by the bite of the cit. SHOOTING POACHERS IN CrrEstrtnE.—Frederick Ayles- bury, head gamekeeper to Lord Egerten of Tetton, was remanded at Altrincbam, on Wednesday, charged with shooting Robert Moss, one of a number of Wien from Wilms- low, who were poaching on Lord Egerton's estite a week ego. It was alleged that the prisoner and other keepers fired at the poachers without any necessity. Moss received the charge from Aylesbury's gun in his legs, and is now in Stockport Infirmary. The case is, on the statement of the poachers a serious one, and will no doubt be thoroughly in- I vestigated. MR. MUNDELL& AND THE UNIONIST CONFERENCE.— OR Tuesday night, at Rhyl, Mr. Mundella spoke at a public meeting to inaugurate the federation of the North Wales Liberal Association. He said he would wish the Liberal Unionists to retutn, and would receive them with open arms, but would not concede any main prieciple or set aside their tried and trusted leader. There was only one way to deal with Ireland. They would not succeed in re- moving Irish discontent unless they allowed to Irishmen the right belonging to all free men of governing themselves in their own fashion. DOUBLE MURDER AND SUICIDE BY A. FATHER.—A man named Wooocock, aged 45, residing at Hoowood, DigleYe drowned kimself and his two children in Bilberry Reservoir. Woodcock had stated to his wife that lie had bad a pound deducted from his wages at the mill where he was employed for damaging a piece of cloth. The children were aged four and two years. One body, that of the elder child, has been recovered. The widow is left with six children. The body of Woodcock, with a child fastened to him by a scarf, was brought to the surface. The childs arms were tightly clasped around the father's neck. THREATENING LORD COLIN CAMPBELL. At Westmin- ster Police Court, on Monday' Thomas John Deller, 19, clerk, a well-dreesed youth, was brought up on a wal rant, charged with demanding by means of a threatening letter £lOO from Lerd Colin Campbell. The letter was as felines: —" Dec. Ist, 1888.—My Lord,—Unless you send £lOO he. fore Friday, 7 p.m., to below address, I shall communicate something to Sir Charles Russell which will eurpriee him, and the result of which will surprise you. Money in Bank of England Notes must be there before Friday. It will be of no use to send before to try and take proceedings against me, as I shall not be there.—Yours, M. 1). D. If you want to win your case, my evidence had beet be unheard. Take the hit."—Lord Colin Campbell deposed to having read the letter. He had no knowledge of the writing. The de-

.•••••I fendant was remanded on bail. -- Tlxn PROSECUTION OF MR. DILLON. -- The proceedings against Mr. John Dillon, M.P., for his advocacy of the "plan of campaign "against Irish landlords were concluded in the Queen's Bench Court in Dublin on Tuesday. Mr. Dillon addressed the Court for about an hour and a half. He argued that if he was guilty Sir Redvers Buller was also guilty, because both were doing the same thing, though by different means—he (Mr. Dillon) by urging the tenants to combine, and General Boller by refusing police protection, and bringing pressure to bear upon the landlords to make .them reduce rack-rents. Whatever the decision of the Court, the work in which he was engaged would still go on. Mr. Justice O'Brien delivered the judgment of the Court. He said the combination in which the defendant was concerned was clearly, distinctly, wad absolutely illegal, and in making this proneuncetnent the Court was exercising, not an au- thority vested in it by ancient statutes, but an inherent authority vested in it by, reason of its undoubted function of preserving the peace and reason, the ;aw of she country. The Court ordered that Mr. Dillon should ithin twelve days give security for £l,OOO, and find two suretiee of ZOO each (a total bail of £2,000) as a guarantee of his good behaviour, or in default undergo six months' imprison- ment.

WESTON RECREATION V. NEWToWN Reattemns.—This match was played at Weston on Saturday, Weston winning by one goal, two tries, and five minors to nil. RUNCORN WANDERERS V. HALTON.—The match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday. Halton were beaten by one try and five minors to two minors. HOWLEY ROVERS V. ORFORD TRUE Beents.—This match was played on Saturday, on the ground of the latter, and resulted in a try for the Rovers to a disputed goal. RUNCORN JOCKEYS V. FRODSHAM ReeiGnas.—A match between these clubs was played at Frodsham on Saturday, ending in the Jockeys scoring 3 goals, 2 tries, and 19 minors to nil. FRODSHAM ROVERS Y. LATCHFORD.—A match was played between these clubs on Saturday at Frodsham, ending in Frodsham scoring 5 minors to Latchford 2 minors. RUNCORN HORNETS V. SIMMS' CROSS Rovnsts.—This match was played on the ground of the former, and ended in a win for the same by 1 goal, 1 try, and 10 minor points to 1 try, 1 disputed try, and 3 minors. STAMFORD RANGERS V. DALLAM LANE AMATEUIts. This match was played on the ground of the latter on Sat-1 urday,'and resulted in a victory for the Rangers by two goals, one try, six minors te three minors. WARRINGTON WANDERERS V. LEAGUE HALL. This match was played on the ground of the former, and was witnessed by 800 spectators. It resulted in an easy Vic- tory for the Wanderers by two tries, five minors to nil. 1 ORFORD TRUE BLUES V. HOWLEY ROVERS —A match I between the above clubs was played on the ground of the I former on Saturday. After a rough and exciting game the True Blues won by one goal (kicked by Branwoodl and two minors to a disputed try. FARNWoRTH V. BIRKENHEAD WANDERERS (I,sT TEAMS). —These teams met on Saturday, on the ground of the for- mer, and, after a very pleasant and well contested game, the result was a draw, Farnworth scoring 1 try and 2 minors to Birkenhead 1 try and 2 minors. • LATCHFORD 2ND V. STAR OF HOPE 2ND TEAM. This match was played at Latchford, on Saturday, and ended in a victory for the home teem by 1 try 2 minors to 3 minors. The try was got by Hartley. Houghton, T. Taylor, Con- nor, and Hartley played well. WARRINGTON RECREATION V. LEIGH FIR LANE.-012 the ground of the former, and after a most exciting game ended in a win for the home team by one goal, one try, to one goal and one minor. Davenport and Forster got the tries for the Rees, and Jackson kicked the goal. WIDNES V. ECCLES.—With a team weakened by the ab- sence of Kiddie, Farrell, Howard, Harding. and Hughes, Widnes journeyed to Eccles on Saturday, and met the club of that town, with whom, notwithstanding that they had their best team on the field, Widnes played a smart and even game, which resulted in favour of Eccles by one try and one minor to one minor. Rusconw v. WIGAN.—The Runcorn fifteen went to Wigan on Saturday with the object of playing off the re- turn fixture with the club of that town. An inspection of the ground revealed thgt it was quite unfit to play upon, the field being covered with mud to the depth of three inches. In order not to dwappoint the large number of spectators who had assembled, the two captains endeavoured to make an arrangement for a drawn game to be played, but the ne- gotiations were unsuccessful, and it is expected that another date'will be given. WIDNES RECREATION V. SWINTON " A " TEAM.—This in- teresting match was played at Widnes on Saturday last; and resulted after a pleasant game in a victory for the Swinton- lens by 1 try and 1 minor peint to Recreation 3 minor points. For Swintom, Hurst, Kenyon, and Hardman in the back division played a grand game, while the best of a good set of forwards were Clayton, Birch, and Scholes. The Recs were best represented by Smith. Grundy, and Rimmer in the back division. and Cosgrove. Flynn, and McCririe in the forwards. Teams:—Widnes Recreation: Wailing, fall back; Smith, Grundy, and Broome, three-quarter backs; Rimrner and Bradshaw, half backs; McCririe, Currie. Flynn, Gregory, Tookies, Norris, Coggrove, Brannon, and Sumner, forwards. Umpire, Mr. A. Critchley. Swinton "A" team: Hurst, full back; Kenyon, Lansd ale, and Lord, three- quarter backs; .Hardman aid Hudson, half backs; Scholes, Hall, Hope. Kenyon, Clayton, Evans, Birch, Harris, and Worthington, forwards. Referee, Mr.- H. Stirrup, Wid- nes F C. COCKIIEDGE MISSION STAR OF HOPE V. PENKETH (IST Two.) —Played on the ground of the former, on Saturday. The home team started the ball, which was immediately re- turned by Aerplaiton. A scrimmaee was formed, when Duni- bell gained possession and passed to Appleton. who struggled over the home line. An appeal was lodged for "forward," and the ball Was brought back and scrimmaged. After some loose play, the Stars took the ball into the visitors' quarters. a minor being the result. On changing ends the ball travelled rapidly trnm post to poet, both a dines at times being endangered. From a scrim maze Whalley gave Hab- berleso a nice pass, the latter player kicking, and following • I well up, was making sure tracks for the visitors' line, being brought down about two yards off by Caldwell. 'The ball travelled back again, when Miles put in a grand run and kick. Rafferty andPhosnix took it over the line, the latter completing the try. Blecitmore took the place and landed a splendid goal. At this point the visitors left the field be- cause the referee allowed the try. This left the home team with another victory to their credit, the score being—Ster of Hope 1 goal 2 minors, Penketh 4 minors. RUNCORN (2ND) V. Wratax (2tien) —The junior teams of the organisations of Runcarn and Wigan met at Runcorn' to play off their return fixture. A good game was anticipated, and the expectations were realised, and the Runcorn team won by one try and four minor points to two minor points. On the side of Runcorn, Rrazendale did his work fairly well. Of the three-quarters Whinyates was decidedly the best nun—be held the ball well and kicked nicely into touch, doing good service on many occasions. Among the forwards Stubbs did a lot of hard, honest forward play, being well supported by Gittins, Cox, and Abrams!' Among the Wigan team Yates at full beck was very safe, William- son and Bootle putting in some very nice pieces of play fre- quently. In the forwards Simms, Hogan, and Grime were most prominent. Teams : Runcorn: Full back. S. Brezendale ; three-quatter becks. E. Lunt, W. A. Riley, end T. Whinyates ; half hicl,e, T. Davies and A. Clare; forwards, W. Dunbayand, J. Giteins, J. Stubbs, W. Kirk- ham, H. Hancock, T. Cox, W. Jones, P. Riley, and T.' Abrams. Wigan: Full back, J. R. Yates;. three-quarter backs, J. Williamson, J. Bootle, and W. France • half backs, J. Mitchinson and W. Baldwin; forwards, C. Simm (captain), G. Fllison, W. Hogan, Carrington, J. Horsfield, J. Hatton, W. S. Finch, P. Clerk, and S. Grime. Sr. PAUL'S Y. PENKETH (2ND TEAMS).—This match was played at Penketh on Saturday, and after a very fast and well-fought game the visitors were victorious. Penketh kicked off at 3-30, Williams returning well to centre, when by hard work the visitots' forwards worked the leather into the home 25, where Williams obtained possession from a scrummage, and passed to A. Jones, Who dropped a good goal. Simpson restarted, but the bell was returned to Pen- keth goal line, where Sinipson obtained a free nick. wbich F. Jones nicely stopped, obtained the ball, and got over the line with a Penketh man, the maul resulting in a minor. After this some give and take play was witnessed which brought about half-time. F. Jones restarted and the Penketh forwards by a good dribble made St.. Paul's goal look dangerous, but A. Jones relieved by a run and kick. After a scrummage Wood got possession, and gained a fine try, which was not, however, converted into the major point. Time was then called, leaving the score—St. Paul's 1 goal 1 try, and 7 minors, to Penketh nil. For the horns team Simpson, Davies, and Forster at back, and Thorpe for- ward played well, whilst St. Paul's played well without an exception, the pick being A. Jones, Wood, Barker, and Williams at back, and Beswick, F. Jones, and Holbrook, for-

wards. SANKEY V. WIGAN NORTH END.—This match was played on Saturday on the Sankey ground. The visitors brought with them a strong team, intending, if possible, to lower the Sankey colours. This they failed to do, and when the match was over Sankey had added another victory to their unbeaten record. The home team kicked off, and as a good return was made, the play for a time was located at the centre, where scrimmaging was indulged in pretty freely. The home ferwards, at length, however, broke away in a nice dribble to near the line, where scrimmaging was again the order of the day, until a minor point relieved the pressure from the visitors. After the drop out, San- key again returned •to the attack, and Ashton got over by a good run. The try, however, was not 'allowed, owing to alleged off-side play. McCann, for the visitors, now put in a good run and kick, and the home team had for a time to act on the defeneive, until the registering of a minor point gave them relief. Nothing more was scored until after half-time, the score then being one minor point each. After the recommencement of the game Sankey soon pressed their opponents, and a touchdown was quickly added to their score. The visitors then managed to get the play to the centre, but Barton replied with a long kick which went into touch at the quaTte.r flag. From the line up the same player again secured the ball, and by means of an excellent run, managed to get over. The try, however, was not allowed, on the plea that the ball had beep grohnded on the line. Soon after this Highley and Dykes came through a scrimmage with the ball at their feet, and took it Over the line, the latter player completing the try.
