div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 18, 1880.

"0. That the acquisition of the Bridgewater undertakings for the sum of .E 1,710,000 fixed by the Act of Parliament would be an advantageous put.- chase for the Ship Canal Company, and that the present average net income of £60,000 would, after the completion of the works, continue to be derived from the Bridgewater Cana" and those other por- tions of the Bridgewater properties not required for the construction of the Ship Canal. "7. That the capital powers of the company, under their Acts of Parliament, amounting to £9,81.2,000, are sufficient for all the purposes con- templated by their .Acts. "8. That the project is a thoroughly sound com- mercial undertaking, and would speedily become remunerative on the completion of the woiks That a large amount of traffic would be at once secured, and that thereafter the increase in traffic and revenue must be steady and continuous. "Having regard to the responsible character of , this report., we feel it our duty to state that in our judgment it is necessary, before the issue of any further prospectus, to reconstitute and greatly to strengthen the Board of Directors." It may be urged that the conclusions of the Consultative Committee do not add anything that is really new as to ti e Ship Canal Scheme ; and that, practically, the same things have been said over and over again by the promoters. The new and important feature, however, is to be found in these things being • stated by a body of men acting outside the promoters, • and after an exhaustive inquiry which has led some amongst their number to change their views as to the commercial character of the un dertaking. There are many opponents of the scheme who are willing to admit that there is no insuperable engineering difficulty i in the way. The canal can be made, but i they ask, " Will it pay when it is made ? This all-important question is answered in the affirmative by the Consultate Commit• tee, who make a noin'. of stating that their conclusions as to the project are far more favourable than they could have anticipated. How far all this is likely to affect investors , remains to be seen. There are few amongst this class who are in a position to spend five weeks in making investigations, and the question with them is whether they will not be justified in letting themselves be influ- enced by those who, without hope of fee or reward, have really done this work in their behalf. The Committee make one sugges- tion which will in all likelihood he welcomed , by the general public; and that is that it is desirable to reconstitute and greatly streng- then the Board of Directors. Mr. ADAMSON, the chairman of the Board, did not show him- self very well pleased with this suggestion at the meeting held in Manchester to receive the report. No one knows better than he 1. the sacrifices of time and money which the members of the present Board have made to bring the project through the ordeals it has al- ready undergone; and we can quite understand • his feeling a trifle irritated at a suggestipn of this kind coming from men who have to con- !, fess that they have not been as quick as the members of the Board in forming an opinion as to the soundness of the undertaking. But on the other hand, Mr. ADAMSON would do well to remember that the stigma , of failure to float the scheme attaches to the • present Board ; for they cannot rid them- selves of the responsibility by saying that that was a matter which they left entirely in the hands of Messrs. Rothschild. It was a mistake to risk, in the circumstances of the ! time, what proved to be such a terrible failure; and it is not unnatural that the in- vesting public should wish to see the Board of Directors re-constituted and strengthened. Confidence in an affair of this kind is well nigh everything. Lack of confidence means a second failure, and a second failure would be the utter ruin of the present project. • There is plenty of money in the market—the I floating of the Guinness Brewery showed that. What the promoters have got to do is to utilise the labours of the Consultative Committee so as to bring the world of in- vestors to their side. It is no use depending on dribblets from working-men. They are good just in so far as "every little helps to make a mickle "; but no farther. The nine millions required for the completion of the Man- chester Ship Canal wiil not be raised in this way. It will have to be raised by the capi • talists of Lancashire themselves subscribing , such a proportion of the whole as will con- vince (residers that there is no timidity— that there is no fear as to the result. The rest of the money will then "flock in," and the job, so far as finance is concerned, will be done without even the aid of a Roths • child.

On Tuesday the Liberals of Notth Wales held a Conference, at Rhyl, with a view to forming a Federation having for its object the advancement of Welsh interests in Par- liament. The Welsh have been very patient, but they are now moving in the wake of Ire- land and of Scotland in formulating their de- mands, and in putting themselves in a posi- tion to enforce them. There was a large amount of business to transact, and want of time only prevented the discussion of a reso- lution moved by Mr. T. E. ELVIS, M.P., affirming that the principle of national self- government should be applied to Wales. Mr. Er.r.ls is a typical Welshman who is thoroughly familiar with the aspirations of his countrymen ; and, judging from the speeches made at the Conference, it is a matter of course to say that Welshmen are in favour of a policy of Home Rule for Wales. Scotland the other week formally put forward her demand for Home Rule, and, as Ireland has been demanding it for some time, it remains only for slow, sleepy England to follow the lead that has been given her. The Conference at Rhyl revealed, too, how much in earnest the Welsh are on the question of Land Law Reform, and the Dises.tablishment of the English Church. The tithe agitation has given a special set to the current of their thought on this question; and if we are not very much mistaken it will operate with Eng- lish farmers in a similar way. With Welsh- men who have their hearts fixed on Disest tb• lishment there is no be,ting about the bush as to Disendowment ; for the resolution passed on Tuesday affirms that "all the tithes orWales should be devoted to matters purely secular within the principality." The Tories are showing themselves anxious to get rid of the tithe question by making it a payment to the landlord. The clergy would no doubt much prefer that they should be relieved of any trouble in the matter; they know it "looks bad" for them to have to di'strain upon people in support of religion, and they would rather have to apply to the landlord for their pound of flesh. Whether, when it comes to legislation on the subject, the landlord will see the issue in the same light is another matter. We are rather disposel to think that a Parliament which contains so many of the landed gentry will hesitate to relieve the clergy of the odium which justly attaches to their mode of raising the principal revenue of the Church. It is beginning to be seen that a bit of hocus-pocus of this kind will,after all, be but a poor sort of tinkering in face of the demand which is now being made in Wales for applying tithf-s to national objects. The Welsh seem to think they could not do better

than apbly the vast sums-derived from this source to educational purposes, and we are inclined to agree with them. It 'would be an , easy way of bringing about Free Education ; and there would be something lef, we should think, for other good objects of a national character. The clergy, will, of course, talk about" spoliation and robbery," just as they did when the Irish Church was disestablished and disendowed ; but, as that did not prevent the right thing being done then, it need not prevent it now. There are some who think it would be wise to abolish tithes altogeth r; but these people do not look far ahead. Tithes are national prN perty ; they must be preserved as such, and applied to national purposes. The Welsh see this ; they mean to make tithes taste sweet rather than bitter, and we conp.-,ratu,ate them alike as to their Ot-esi?ht and determi- nation.

other chief apartments are spacious, lit by fine Tudor windows deeply embayed and elegantly ap; pointed. Tile Library contains the subscription portrait of Lord Winmarleigh in his uniform of the rd Royal Lancashire Militia—a portrait which be- longs to the regiment, and numerous other portraits, old and by modern artists. The situation of Win- marleigh House has been judiciously chosen. The ground naturally undulates slightly, and the soil is a rich loam, with porous subsoil, upon a deep bed of gravel. The grounds were laid out by Mr. Thomas, the now rather celebrated landscape gar- dener. The gardens, shrubberies, and surrounding plantations have been planned in the most effective manner. The kitchen gardens and conservatories are ample. The evergreen shrubs, after being plan- ted little more than ten years, are flourishing won- derfully. Winmarleigh has already assumed a charming aspect. even when visited in mid-winter; and as the trees grow and nature puts her finishing touches to the picture, the • latest seat of the ennobled family of the Fattens will become one of the most attractive spots in the county. From the garden A alks at the front of the house, the prospect to the eastward where the plain is bounded by the lofty and shapely Fells of Bleasdale, is exceed- ingly impressive. The estate, fairly well timbered, affords, a pleasing foreground and middle distance. The house was built in the year 1871 ; that, at least, is the date cut in stone upon the porch, with the initials of the builder and master—"J.W.P." (John Wilson-Patten.) Lord Winmarleigh has not been unmindful of the claims of the tenantry and cottagers upon his estate, in regard to religious and educational provision. A pretty little Church, erected in 1876, dedicated to St. Luke, containing 160 sittings, all of which are free, with a living of which his lordship is patron, stands by the road-side not far from the mansion: and a little further on there is a village school- house. Thus, with a kind landlord, whose daughters pay great attention to the physi- cal and moral wants of the peasantry, with a church, a school, a parsonage, a vicar, and a schoolmaster (or mistress), Winmarleigh in 1886 may deem itself fortunate in circumstances, and well to the fore in al civilising and humanising agencies.

This week we present each purchaser of " The Examiner"' with a large sheet Almanac, printed in two colours, which, in addition to containing a large amount of local and general information, is embellished with illustrations of Winmarleigh House, and a portrait of Lord Winmarleigh. Be- low we furnish a brief historical account of Win- marleigh House and Manor, and a sketch of the career of Lord Wiumarleigh. WINMARLEIGH HOUSE AND MANOR.

WINAIARLEIGH is the name of a sequestered j township in the Fylde country of North Lancashire, I situate two to three miles westward of the great high-road from Preston and the country to the south to Lancaster and the north. It contains a population of no more than some three hundred souls, domiciled in about fifty dwellings, farm- , houses and cottages for the most part. The occu- pation of the inhabitants is husbandry or agricul- tuee. Less than 20 years ago there was no building lor natural or artificial feature in the township , which the most observant of travellers through the , Idistrict would have turned aside to see. At last : the place was retrieved from its age-long obscurity and insignificance by becoming the home of a pro- prietor who had attained a national reputation as a politician, as well as a social eminence as the pro- moter of many movements for the public welfare, and the name of Witimarleigh was brought into familiar usage in the Imperial Parliament and the highest circles, royal and aristocratic, as part of the titular designation of a nobleman whom all Eng- land knows and respects, and whom Lancashire men in particular delight to honour as a native of the County Palatine, whose public life has been so intimately associated with the history of this im- portant province ot England. The name is one which has undergone many var- iations from its original orthography. It is spelt at least twenty different ways, from" Wimerlegh," in the reign of Henry 111, (A.D. 1241), and "Wynmerles" a century later (1343), to " Winmerle " in 1476 ; " Wilmerlegh" in 1500; " Wymmersley" in 1561 ; and" Winmerley " in 1668; and " Winmarley " and " Wiemarleigh ' in the present century. Although the recorded history of a rural town- ship like this is almost nil, yet there are interesting relics of prehistoric times in this particular neigh- bourhood, some of srhich have been deposited for exhibition in the public museum at Warrington, and others are .preserved by Lord Winin.arleigh, out of whose land they were dug up. Of the earliest owners of the manor estate of Win- marleigh mentioned in ancient documents, it may be remarked that they bore the township name as their surname; and that when they passed away, a daughter and heiress of the ' last of them, Roger de Wynmarleigh, married Henry de Plesington, lord of Plesin.ston, near Blackburn, and their daughter and heiress, Isabella de Plesing,ton, became the wife of Richard de Radcliffe, who with her had the manor of Winmarleigh with other estates. The Radcliffes first appear as lords of Win- marleigh in the second half of the fourteenth 'cen- tury; and they continued in a male succession to hold this manor during about, two hundred years, until the reign of Queen Elizabeth in the latter part of the sixteenth century. Sir Gilbert Gerard, Kt. some time Attorney-Gen- eral and master of the Rolls, hold iViumarleigh in right of his wife, Anne Radcliffe. Sir Gilbert Ger- ard died in 1592; and the estate passed to his son and heir, Sir Thomas Gerard, created, in 1603, Baron Gerard of Gerards, Bromley. Winmarleigh after- wards became the inheritance sf Elizabeth Gerard, (laughter of Dutton, Lord Gerard; she married the Hon. William Spencer, of Ashton Hall near Lancas- ter, and bore issue William Spencer, whose daughter J Elizabeth became wife of R Theft Hesketh, Esq., of Rufford, and the only child of this marriage, Eliza- beth Hesketh, married, in 1714, Sir Edward Stanley. afterwards eleventh Earl of Derby. It was in order to raise money to pay Lady Derby's portion, says the historiairof Garstang parish (Mr. Fishwick), that the Spencer family sold, in 1763, the Winmar- leigh manor estate to Thomas Patten, Esq., of Bank Hall, in Warrington, by deed dated 18 and 19 March, 1744. Thus, the Pattens have owned Winmarleigh, nearly 150 years. Winmarleigh Hall, the old manor-house, long the domicile of the Radcliffes, having ceased to be the residence of the lords of the Manor after the death of William Radcliffe, Esq., in 1560, had fallen into neglect and decay. No doubt it was used for a farmhouse until being dilapidated, it was de- molished, in the latter end of last century, and upon its site another house was built, which is the farmhouse of the home-farm formed under the direction of Lord Winmarleigh himself. The situation of this structure and the site of the old Hall is a few hundred yards away from the modern mansion close by the entrance to the grounds from the public road. The farmhouse has of course no historic interest, but there is an ancient yew:tree in the orchard near the house, which may I have been planted by a former lord' of Winmarleigh who dwelt in the manor-house. The land of the hall-farm includes some of the best on the estate. Respecting one field, there is a tradition that in a certain year when corn was at its highest price, probably in the war-time seventy or eighty years since, the crop of wheat ,c.,Town upon it yielded when sold a sum equal to the estimated value of the fee-Simple of the land. Lord Winmarleigh (then Colonel Wilson-Patten) used to spend some two Gr three months of every year in the neighbourhood, shooting over the Win- marleigh estate, which is plentifully stocked with game, for a number of years before he entertained an idea of building a mansion there that should be- come the future family seat. We have now to append a brief and general. description of Winmarleigh House, the new seat of Lord Winmarleigh. Our engraving will convey a better idea of its character than any verbal sketch. The house consists chiefly of two oblong blocks of: building set at right angles to each other. The front 'of the house is shown in the smaller woodcut, after a photograph taken from the south-west angle. It presents a good architectural aspect em- boldened by projecting bays on two storeys, having large windows, mullioned and transomed, and ter- minating in a handsome parapet on Gothic stone- work at the east end of the frontage, and in a gabled upper storey at the ,end. The style is domestic Elizabethan, and the materials used externally are red bricks and fine freestone. The stonework is enriched by sculptured heraldic shields and other , appropriate devices. The other block, of consider- able length, extending from the back of the princi- pal building, is exhibited in our larger engraving, j also from a photograph. Its salient feature is the main entrance to the house, underneath a tine porch, having two Tudor-arched doorways, above which the walls are decorated with mouldings and carved panels, and finished with arcaded para- pets, flanked by turreted buttresses. Behind the porch', covering the entrance hall, rises a square tower of three stories, its front pierced with win- dows, the larger one on the first floor molioned and transomed. The tower has bold pillared parapets, and a roof of high-pitched pyramidial form, in the centre of which a weather vane is fixed. The tower is flanked by corbelled chimneys, and dominates the other structure from any point of view. Large and handsomely designed chimneys rise from the gables and roof-ridges, as shown. in the engraving; and, together with the several gabled buildings of diffler- ent elevations, the tower, roof, gablets, &sc., impart that picturesqueness of sky-line which constitutes the peculiar beauty of Gothic architecture in all its uses, whether for ecclesiastical, civic, or domestic edifices. Mr. Paley, of Lancaster, was the architect of Winmarleigh House, and it is a work which does credit to its designer. It is not ambitious in scale, elaborate in plan, or overplied with ornamentation in detail, but it is a beautiful country house, worthy of its patrician owner. Respecting the interior, we fan but say that the library, drawing-room, and

Winmarleigh of Winmarleigh in the county of Lan- caster. Long and eminent as have been the services rendered to the country generally, and to Lan- cashire especially, in both Houses of Parliament, these do not by any means exhaust the duties of citizenship energetically and ably discharged by his lordship. During a period of sixty years he served in the various ranks of the Militia service ; fifty- five years in the 3rd Royal Lancashire Regiment, of which thirty as Colonel commanding, and thirteen as honorary Colonel. In 1855 Col. Wilson-Patten accompanied the Regiment 60 Gibraltar, during the Crimean War, and on his return his services were favourably mentioned by Her Majesty's Government ill both Houses of Parliament; and Her Majesty was graciously pleased to appoint him one of her aides-de-camp, of whom his lordship is now the senior. In Lancashire, Lord Winmarleigh has beenl conspicuous as a promoter of improved methods in ; agriculture, and the county and local agricultural societies have found in him a liberal and zealous patron. On the occurrence of what is known as the Cotton Famine, in 1862-65, his lordship, then Colonel Wilson-Patten, showed his hearty and prac- tical sympathy with the suffering operatives by presiding over the first public meeting to raise sub- scriptions for the relief of the unemployed work- people in the cotton manufacturing districts, and during the whole period of that calamity he served on the Central Committee at. Manchester, under the presidency of the late, Lord Derby. The last few years of his lordship's life have been spent in a dignified retirement at Winmarleigh. The storms of party-political warfare are over for the veteran, who will have attained his eighty-fifth year in April next Notwithstanding his advanced age, however, Lord Winmarleigh still not infrequently takes a prominent part in gatherings of a public character, and, as an instance, it may be mentioned that last week he took part in a meeting held at Warrington of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society, and subse- quently presided at the luncheon. On the occasion of its last show at Chester, this Society presented -Lord Winmarleigh with a piece of plate, and an illu- minated address, which cost the sum of 200 guineas, as ft mark of "well-deserved recognition of long and ' influential service in its favour." Our readers will join us in the hope that he will be long spared to give the benefit of his ripe experience to this and other useful institutions.

WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. A meeting was held in Al;orde Chambers, on Wednesday. Mr. H. IV. Deacon presided, and there were preseut Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. S. Sadler, R. Lewis, J. Morrison, B. Brown, S. Rob- inson, and J. 'l'. Allen (clerk to the Local Board.) A com- mittee consisting of the chairman and Messrs. Morrison and Robinson had been appointed to make a selection of books, and they presented a list of about 2,000 which was ap- proved. The probable cost will be abeut £3OO. This was the only business of interest. SIMMS CROSS PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, WIDNES. —This edifice, which is also used as a school, has recently undergone considerable renovation and extension. The most important alteration is the addition of several class- rooms to the building, and the accommodation has been cousiderablvoimproved. Re-opening services were held on Sunday, wt-11 the Rev. T. Dain preached morning and eveniog to large congregations. On Monday evening the rev, gentleman delivered an amusing and instructive lecture on" Habits, good and indifferent." There was only a mo- derate attendance. The Rev. J. Calvert presided. " FUNERAL AT HALTON.—The funeral of the late Mr. John Haddock, formerly of Halton-road, Runcorn, took place on Sunday afternoon at the new cemetery, Halton. The mem- bers of the senior class at the Trinity Weeleyan Sunday school, Halton, to which the deceased formerly belonged, besides several residents, preceded the hearse. M. Mad- dock was the first member of the Halton tent of the Inde- pendent Order of Rechabites, and the members of the tent together with those of the Union (Runcorn) tent, also tot, lowed the body to the wave. In Halton the whole of the scholars belonging to the Halton Wesleyan Sunday School met the body and preceded it to the Wesleyan Chapel, where a short service was conducted by the Rev. R. F. Hornabrook. Most of the residents had drawn the blinds of their windows, and the ceremony in the cemetery was wit- nessed by a large number of spectators. The burial service was conducted by the Rev. R. F. Elornabrook. It may be mentioned that the deceased was the first adult buried in the new cemetery. The hearse and mourning coaches were supplied by Mr. S. Yarwood, of Runcatrn. A ST. HELENS CONTRACTOR FINED FOE CreetErrY.— Before Celonel Gamble and Mr. T. S. Timmis, at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, William Mercer, a carter, was chaTged with cruelly ill-treating a horse by working it whilst in an unfit state. Joseph Benuion, contractor, St. Helens, was charged with allowing the horse to be so worked.— P.C. Almond deposed that on the 3rd lust he saw Mercer in Birchtl.ld-road, Widnes, in charge of three horses and a lorry, which was loaded with a large caustic pan. He ex- amined the shaft horse, and under the saddle found a sore almost as large as the palm of his band. There was blood and matter coming from it. The constable afterwards saw defendant Bennion at St. Helens, and the latter stated that " it was only a bit of a sore in the morning."—lnspector Wood said the horse was in a low condition, and he consi- dered it gross cruelty to work a horse in that state.—De- fendattt said he was obliged to work the horse, because he was so wicked, and they could not do anything with him otherwise.—Bennion was fined LI and costs, and his man was mulcted in the sum of 2s 6d and costs, 2s 6d. THE MYSTERIOUS DROWNING CASE WE WIDNES.—Tbe inquest on the body of James Perry, a sailor on board the steamer Kangaroo, of Douglas, Isle of Man, who was drowned in the West Bank Dock, on Friday last, under somewhat mysterious circumstances, was held at the Arab Hotel, on Monday afternoon. Mr. James White occupied the chair, and among-t those present were Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P, and Mr. J Edwards-Moss. The member delivered an address, in which lie expressed his concurrence with the attempt to form a club, and dwelt upon the advantages of such an institution. It was stated that the company was intended to be formed in 2,000 shares of £1 each, and Mr. R. Lewis informed the meeting that they would probably have to speed £BOO for the building, £4OO for land, and £3OO or £4BO for furnirhing, in order to make, the club as useful and camfortable as it should le.—Mr.flohn Edwards-Moss also delivered an addresss. The purpose of the promoters was to obtain money to pay off a mortgage of £3OO on the minister's manse belonging to Bethesda C.hapel, and also to enable the latter building to be repaired and renovated. The object was fully attained. The total amount realised was upwards 1 of £4OO, and this sum included the following donations : Mr. Hobert Verdin, M.P. £2O; Mr. James Handley, J.P , £2O • Mr. P. Speakman, £10; Mr. F. Fairhurst, £10; Mr. J. T. Brunner, £5; Mr. R. Shaw. £3; and Dr. Mackie, £2 2s. SATURDAY, DECEMBER 18, 1886.

THE Manchestv Ship Canal Scheme has been little heard of for the past few weeks— so little, in fact, that its enemies were be- ginning to say that in a little time 'nothing would be heard of it at all. It has not, how- ever, been lost sight of, and it is again before the public, A Consultative Committee was, it will be remembered, appointed to inquire into the soundness and general character of the undertaking when it was found that Messrs. ROTHSCHILD had failed to float the scherne. It was felt that if the confidence of the Public was to be secured, there must be an expression of opinion in favour of the pro- ject coming from well-qualifidt men who had made an investigation apart from the promo- ters. To this end the Consultative Commit- tee was appointed; and it is due to that , bodY, and to the scheme itself, to say that they did not commence their labours with preconceptions ; that their investigation has been laborious and pains-taking; and that the are chief result of their inquiry is that they led to unanimously recommend the scheme as a sound commercial under- taking. The sittings of the Committee have extended over a period of five weeks : there , have been no less than fourteen meetings, I and no single meeting has lasted less than four hours. It will be seen, therefore, that the conclusions arrived at have not been has- tily formed; and, proceeding as they do from business men accustomed to consider- ing details; they will undoubtedly have great weight with the public. The Commit- tee give th conclusions in the following terms : "1. That the Ship Canal and Works are practic- able from an, ellineering point of view, and would permit vessels el the largest class to be safely navi- gated to and from Manchester. , "2. That e Canal and works can be completed ready for Mime at a cost within the estimate of £5.750,000, and that the sum of £802,936 set down for the purchase of the necessary land is a safe estimate. " Canal and works should be eon- stru3c.tedTiularidetrhe a Contract fixing a maximum sum, any possibility of the estimate bineionrgdeerxeteoepdreert "4. That graving dock accommodation should be provided, and be ready for use on the opening of , the canal. I "5. That the estimate of £104,200 per annum for the expenses of the working and maintenance is ample. There 'would probably be a material sav- ing on this item during the first few years after completion,

div.head: LORD WIN'MARLEIGH. -f us
div.p: LORD WIN'MARLEIGH. -f us

The illustration ot our almanac also contains an engraved portrait of Lord Winmarleigh. It may be re- garded as a good likeness, representing faithfully the finely-cut features of his lordship, so familiar to many of our readers who have seen Lord I% inmar- , leigh upon public occasions. We do not purpose to ' give anything like a full biographical sketch to accompany the portrait, but merely to allude to the local connection of his lordship, and draw an out- line of his unusually long and active public career. The family to which Lord Winmarleigh belongs is mentioned, we are told, by Stow, in the celebrated roll of Battle Abbey, among those who came over to England with William the Conqueror. For many generations the family was closely connected by ' residence with Warrington and neighbourhood, the present Lord Winmarleigh, then Colonel Wilson ! Patten, only removing from Bank Hall to his new mansion at Winmarleigh some fourteen or fifteen years ago. At that time there was a pretty general feeling in favour of a Town Hall and Park being procured for Warrington, and Colonel Wilson-Patten , intimated to the Corporation that he would be pre- pared to make some personal and pecuniary sacri- fice if he could thereby secure to his fellow-towns- men the possession of Bank Hall and Gardens as a Town Hall and Park. Steps were at once taken by the Corporation, with the result that Warrington became the possessor of its present Town Hall and , beautiful gardens, towards the cost of which I Mr. George Crosfield munificently gave .£9,500, and Colonel Wilson - Patten .E 3,000. We may add that Lord Winmarleigh's father was a man of note in the county. He was Thomas Wilson- Patten, Esq., M.P., who was born on the 22nd of IFebruary, 1770, and assumed the additional sur- name of Wilson on succeeding by the will of the Rev. Thomas Wilson, Prebend of Westminster, to estates in Lancashire and Cheshire, the former of which had belonged to the celebrated Bishop Wil- son, of the Isle of Man. Thomas Wilson-Patten, ' Esq., married, March 29th, 1800. Elizabeth, eldest daughter of Nathaniel Hyde, ' Esq., of Ardwick. , There were issue of this union two children, son ' and daughter. The son was John Wilson-Patten, who was born on the 26th of April, 1802; and the daughter was Elizabeth Patten, born in September, 11803, who married, in June, 1823, Sir John Buller I Yarde-Buller, Baronet, of Lupton House, county Devon; he was raised to the peerage as Baron Churston, 2nd August, 1858. The father, Thomas Wilson-Patten, Esq., who had been Lieut.-Colonel of the sth Royal Lancashire Militia, died, aged 57 years, on the 7th December, 1827. His son and heir was at the time of his succession about 25 years of age, so that, within one year, Lord Winmarleigh has held the family estates during the lengthened term of 60 years. John Wilson-Patten was educated at Eton and at Magdalen College, Oxford. On leav- ing Oxford he spent three years in visiting foreign countries; his father was yet living when Mr. Wilson-Patten was performing his travels. Returning to England, and entering into possession of his inheritance, he married, on the 15th April,/ 1828, his cousin, Anna Maria Patten, fourth daughter and co-heiress of Peter Patten-Bold, Esq.. of Bold, in Lancashire. By her he had issue. sons, Eustace John, born Bth Feb., 1836; and Arthur, born 4th Jan., 1840, who entered the army, was a lieutenant in the first battalion of the Rifle Brigade, and died in Canada, unmarried, 2nd Jan., 1866. The daughters were Anna Maria, married to Rev. Robert Rolleston, Rector of Stanford Rivers, Essex, and died in 1869; Ellinor Venda, married to T. H. Lyon, Esq., of Ap- pleton Hall, co. Chester, and died in 1861; and Eliz- abeth. The eldest son, Enstace John Wilson-Pat- ten, captain in the Ist Life Guards, married 12th August, 1863. Emily Constantia, daughter of the Rev. Lord John Thynne, and had issue, a son, John Alfred, born 24th Oct., 1867, and daughters, Con- stance Ellinor and Evelyn Louisa. LordWinmarleigh's 'eldest son died recently and his only son is now • heir to his grandsire. Lord Winmarleigh com- menced his Parliamentary service in the old unre- formed House of Commons, in the year 1830, when he was elected one of the representatives for the , County Palatine of Lancaster, which was then un- divided. His lordship entered Parliament as a Conservative. On the introduction of the first re- form Bill, he voted for its second reading, but feel- ing unable to pledge himself beforehand to all its details, he was obliged, on the dissolution of Parlia- ment in 1831, to yield to the strong expression of public feeling in favour of "The Bill, the whole Bill and nothing but the Bill," and retired. His ab- sence from Parliament was brief. In 1832, the County of Lancaster having been divided by the Reform Act, Mr. Wilson-Patten was invited to stand for the Northern Division together with the late Earl of Derby, then Lord Stanley, and was elected nnopposed. From this date onward he sat as Member for North Lancashire uninterrup- tedly, in the Parliaments elected in 1832, ; 1835, 1837, 1841, 1647, 1852,1857, 1859, and 1665— that is to say, in nine successive Parliaments, ex- tending over a period of thirty-three years. Nor ; does this statement complete the record, for en the division of North Lancashire into •two parts by the : Reform Act of 1867, which came into effect before ' the dilection for 1868, Colonel Wilson-Patten elected to stand for the Northern Division, and was again elected andsat in the House of Commons until his elevation to the Upper House in 1874. Lord Win- marleigh is one of the \few surviving public men -whos-. Parliamentary recollections go back beyond the Reform of 1832. During the Parliament which followed the General Election of 1832, Mr. Wilson- Patten was a supporter of the late Sir Robert Peel till the time of his death. When the great states- man resolved to repeal the Corn Laws in 1846., Mr. Wilson-Patten gave him valuable help, and as a consequence, at the General Election in 1847, he lost the support of some influential men of his party in the county who remained Protectionists, notably of the la e Mr, Robert Townley Parker, of Cuerden. But, as a matter of course, be was re-elected, with Mr. James Heywood, a Liberal Free Trader, for his colleague. Mr. Wilson-Patten took a leading part in the promotion of all measures affecting the com- merce and manufactures of the country and of Lan- cashire.; especially in the repeal of the heavy duty on cotton prints. He seconded the motion for the abolition of the truck system, which for many years had caused great discontent smongst the labouring classes. He carried a bill through Parliament for the closing of public-houses during a portion of Sunday, which, however, was defeated subsequently in consequence of a reaction in the public mind. In 1852, Mr. Wilson-Patten was ap- pointed Chairman of Committees of the House of Commons, during the tenure of which office, and as Chairman of the Committee on Standing Orders, he effected seVeral improvements in the conduct of legislation by private bills. In 1866, he was appointed Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster in Lord Derby's Government, and was created a Member of Her Ma- jesty's Privy. Council. In 1868. he was appointed by Mr. Disraeli Chief Secretary for Ireland, with a seat in the Cabinet. In 1874, Colonel Wilson-Patten . was raised to the Peerage with the title of Baron

In ABSENTsll:—Jirnes Limas, a soldier, was charged with drawing they had been particularly successful. being actabsentee front his regiment, stationed at Chester. They hadobtained 120 certificates from South Ken- He was remanded to the military antiorites. Ken- sington; 12 students had obtained full drawing cer- tificates, which meant that they had passed during the two years they had been at the school five dis- tinct and different examinations in five different branches of drawing. They had also gained 28 prizes from South Kensington for drawing. They were particularly successful in the examination which Dr. Stainer held in the practical knowledge of music. Out of the 48 students who were presen- ted to him, 23 passed "excellent," and 12 out of the 23 obtained the fullest marks which could be ob- tained. (Applause.) The Bishop of Cneeweli, in-the course of an interesting address, said that the longer one lived the more difficult it was to know how propeily to commence a speech. The difficulty arose with the first words, He was told that in these days he was not to say 'ladies and geetlemen," be. cense they were all working-men and workleg-wonien— (laughter)--,-ancl he was told not to say "young ladies," be- cause that meant a particular class in which schoolmis- tresses and intending schoelmiatresses were not included. He was in these days quite prepared, when he went to a railway station, for the porter to address him as a working- mae rather than as " Inv lord." That was it thin, 'hat was coming, and if people would only recognise the fact that he was a working-man he should accept it as a compliment. (Laughter and cheers.) Having congratulated the students on their success the Bishop said that after coegratuletiens a reaction set in, and one felt depres.aed. No doubt there wee depression in the air, and there was a general feel- ing of depression throughout the country. The remedy for depression was philosophy. If he was a philosopher wretch he was not he should put what he had. to say under three heeds—evolution natural selection, and the servival of the fittest. When he *as a boy there was a thing known as , education; when he grew up to be a young man there was 1 a thing known as development, and now that he was gel\ lug very white there was a thing popularly known as evolution. It seemed to him that the three were much the same sortot thing under different names, but at all events they- would serve as a point upon which to hang a few remarks. They students had got to evolve a great deal of knowledge out of books and their own minds, and in time would give it So their pupils, thus evolving good men and woolen, good churchmen and good churchwomen, and good Christians. (Cheers.) Whatever philosophers might say, evolution was not a mere matter of mechanical working. for, as in their case, it meant taking in a great deal befoie they c mld throw out a great deal. When they left °liege they would not be prepared to ti;lit the whole world with the know- ledge they bad acquired. Natural selection then came in, and, in the case of molititook the form of competitive ex- aniinatiens. They most be prepared not always to be at the top of the tree, and net always to see those who were best in that and other professioes awarded with the highest place. The time that was coming would be a trying one for both men and women, and it might b 3 that a far greater 'share of the work of the next thirte years would fell upon women than had ever hitherto been the case. The influence exercised by women was often more effective I than that . exercised by men, and it was a I great hope for the future, if women were ' to have the influence their advocates were pleading fur. They might look with hope ripen that influ- ence being exercised in the canes of purity. honesty, and religion. (Cheers.) Therefore he might urge them to guide their Own lives in such a way that they might afterwards guide the lives of their pupils. There was also a survival of the fittest. There was a rainy day corning for all, and there was no class of people in the country for which the rainy day was more terribly desola- ting than it was for the teaching class, for they knew they could not go on teaching all their lives, and the namel leeson they should draw about the survival of the fittest was that as soon as they began to have schools of their own, they should begin to subscribe to some teechers' pension fund, of which, he was glad to say, there were many in the country. The Bishop then distributed the prizes, and was afterwards cordially thanked on the motion of Canon LONG, seconded by Dr. WATKINS, and supported by Canon BLENCOWE. • The following students took prizes :—Seniors: Holy scrip- ture, Harriet Glover and Margaret Stormont; Prayer Book, Jane Cheetham ; arithmetic, Mary Barrow ; grammar and composition, Margaret Stormant ; geography, Hannah Long- ford and Rhoda Nuttall; English history, Mary Barron; , domestic ecimomy and echool management, Rhoda huttall ; penmanship, Jessie Maxten ; needlework, Jane Challenor„ Margaret Samuel, and Phcebe Holland; music Grace Spencer ; agriculture, Mary 'Jiggle; botany, Rhoda Nut- tall. THE DROWNING FATALITIES *ON THE MERSEY. INQUEST AT PENKETH.

An inquest was held on Atonality afternoon at the ited Lion inn, Penketh, by Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, as to the death, by drowning on the Mersey, of Robert Holden, and Bob Holden, his son. Mr. q. Falba., of Widnes, was present on behalf of the owners of the flat.—lt was stated by James Holden that ' Robert Holden tWas his father, and was 55 years of age, ahil Bob Holden, his brother, was 19, and lived I with his father in Warrington-road, Penketh. Witness's I father, his brother, a man named Whelan, and witness started from Easthem at half-past six on Thursday morn- ing for Widnes with a pargo of sand. His father was the • captain of the flat, which was called "The Dan," and be. ' longed to Messrs. Hill and Grundy, St. Helens. The ; weight of cargo on board was about 85 tons, but it was registered.to carry 100 tons. They bad been sailing with the flood for aboat an boar, and there was a head wind blowing very leeavi:y. They were sailing with double-reefed ' mainsail ana foresail. A sea rushed right over the middle of the vessel and broke the hatches; in. Witness'afather and brother were at the tiller, and witness was forward. In about ten minutes the vessel began to sink, and a steamer I milled the Bridgewater Came in sight and took him off, after he had missed a rope that was thrown to him. By I that time, his father ad brother had gone off the boom end at the ',Teel. He himself was taken off the rigging. lie lied sailed in the flat for four years, and had no fault to find With her equipment, and cansidered her to be thoroughly flels-g'lng- He thought the flat was wrecked in consequence of the extraordinary stormy weather. One of the jurymen said he did not think it was necessary to ask any questions. He was out himself on tire day named, and had never experienced such Weather in the Mersey before.—Witness, in answer to Ser- geant Cairns, said he was present when the bodies of his father and brother were iecovered. Whelan's body had not been recovered. The bodies were found on a bank sur- rounded with water.—John Holding said he lived on the 'Warringt'on-road, Penketb. and was employed by the St. Helens Lighterage Company, and was captain of the steam fat Warrington. On Thursday morning, about seven o'clock, he left the Alexandria Dock pier,Liyerpool. When off Eastharn be noticed a sailing fiat going ahead, and the weather was very stormy. She appeared te be in distress. This would be about half-past eight o'clock. He made to- wards her, and eot within 200 or 300 yards of her; but the Warrington shipped a heavy sea, which washed every- thing movable overboard, the vessel's boats included. One of the ropes got fast with the propeller of the Warrington, and stopped the engines, and compelled witness to let go kis anchor, and he could get no nearer the sailing flat, Which he made oat to be the flat Dan, which he knew to be ittianned by Robt. Holden, sen., his son, James Holden, and Bob Holden. Before witness let go the anchor the Dan had not sunk ; but directly after the anchor was secured he saw the flet sink. One of the men on board got Into the rietzine, and two upon the boom. In five minutes afterwards, if he could have got up to the fiat, 41e. should have been able to have rescued the whole of the men. Wit- ness directed his attention to obtaining assistance, and blew a whistle for tbree-qnarters of an hour. He then VIVI three or four steamers at a distance of about two miles; but they did not alter their course. A steam flat engaged in the salt trade, appeared on the scene and attempted for full twenty minutes to effect a rescue; but the wind being so ""ng, carried the vessel away at each attempt they made, consequently the men on board it were unable to do any- thing to save the deceased. The salt vessel than went for the Bridgew titer steam tug "Bridgewater," which was tow- ing two fiats, and the last witness was rescued. Witness did not see the deceased washed overheard and drowned. Witness V 145 benumbed with cold, as the weather was some- thing fearful. He had been a sailor for something. like 35 years, aid daring that time bad never experienced such a gale in the Mersey.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that deceased were accidentally drowned.—Subse- quently a collection was made among the jurymen, and the etim of 30s was subscribed far the benefit of the be- reaved relatives. • The funeral of Captain R. Holden and his son took place on Tuesday afternoon at the Sankey Cemetery. The hearse and mourning coach were supplied ley Mr. Connor, of War- rington, and there were about fifty or sixty people present, though the weather TM very inclement. The Rev. E. 8. Jackson, vicar, officiated in a edema and impressive II lamer.

LONDON, THURSDAY.

Xetteis )0 the *Wier. MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND no, LIBERAL UNIONISTS. Sir,—l have read your article in last Saturday's issue with some amount of pain, and also your reference a to the Unionisls for a long time as being unfair. 'Jou devote a deal of your space to criticisiog the Unionists, and your enmity seems to be showered mostly on Mr. Chamberlain. And why? because he maintains that politics and consis- tency should go hand in hand together. His conduct can be defended with consistency, while Mr. Gladstone's cannot. But because Mr. Chamberlain terms the followers of Mr. Gladstone's policy on the Irish question as Separatists, you are offended. There is no man who has so clearly proved that the policy of Mr. Gladstone means nothing less than Separation. Mr. Chamberlain endoubtedly has grasped the subject in such a clear light that his speeches from the day they have been delivered have never answered. The more the subject is considered the deeper becomes the conviction, as to Mr. Gladstone'a measures if passed, that the ink would scarcely be dry before Separation was demanded, or if not demanded, all the obligations would be removed. Tbey would be very careful to see that we had the expense of the Army and Navy cast upon the already over-burdened shoulders of the taxpayers of Great Britain. As far as the term Separatists goes I shall never cease using the term, not because of malice and envy, but because Ciladstonian policy means nothing else. You have devoted scarcely any space to the Unionist conference, whereas the space you devote for the purpose of criticising them is any- thing but fair, and considering that we are Liberals as well as you, you ought not to be biassed as to space. When Mr. Chamberlain came to Warrington, Mr. McMinnies in intro- ducing him to the meeting said that Mr. Chamberlain was the beet abused man in Great Britain, but he was not afraid. Alas what a chauge ; and now we find his friends full of scurrilous abuse towards him, and for no other purpose but being consistent. Really, where are we to look for manly criticism, when men professing to be called Liberals carry on I such an unworthy warfare. To my mind Mr. Chamberlain has exhibited an immense amount of patience, at the con- duct of those who should be his friends --I remain, yours &c. RADICAL UNIONIST. [Our correspondent is entitled to his opinion—this is a free country. As to being biassed as to space," we certainly are "biassed " to this extent that, as the Liberal Unionists are a section only of the Liberal party, their doings are not quite so important as are those of the main body. ED. Exl

On Wednesday all the London papers having cor- respondents at Vienna announced that the Bul- garian deputation had offered the vacant throne to Prince Ferdinand of Coburg, news sufficiently in- teresting of itself. But the enterprise of other newspapers was overshadowed by the "Times," which added that in conditionally accepting the proposal, Prince Ferdinand had stated that he be- lieved his candidature would be approved not only . by the Emperor of Austria, but by the Czar. The importance of this condition was recognised by the " Times " in a leading article, wherein it was justly pointed out that, accepting the statement as accu- rate, the Bulgarian difficulty was closed, and the peace of Europe assured. The news was as amazing as it was gratifying. Unfortunately everything ! was true about the statement save the postcript. The " Times " to-day has not a word to say on its sensational announcement of yesterday. Other news from Vienna published this mornnig shows , that the main and critical point is untouched. Bulgaria has invited Prince Ferdinand to the throne. Austria, naturally, will not object; but the Czar has not yet spoken. Upon his mood hangs the issues of peace or war. If he accepts the new can- didate a gr ,at load will be lifted from the mind of Europe. If, as is more probable, he refuses con- sent, the Bulgarian difficulty will remain open, and the dreaded war may come in the spring. It is a pitiful thing to think that these great issues rest upon the caprices or passion of a single man, and he, according to reliable accounts, not quite sane. The plans of the Government in view of next ses- sion are now practically determined. The first business will be Procedure, and there is a strong feeling in the Cabinet in favour of asking the House to give the whole of its time to this business till it shall be disposed of. There will be trouble in any circumstances. But if this proposal be made it will be considerably extended. Mr. Labouchere and some other irreconcileables are determined to oppose Parliamentary Procedure simply because it is pro- posed by a Conservative Government. In this de- tormination they will not find approval with Mr. Gladstone and the leaders of the Liberal party. The Liberals, under Mr. Gladstone's leadership, fought hard to secure the closure and were defeated by Lord Randolph Churchill and his colleagues in the present Government. But the closure is none the less a good thing because it has now been taken up by its former opponents—will certainly not be resisted from the front Opposition bench. Butt° take the whole time of the House is another thing, the mere suggestion of which has excited the righteous ire of Mr. Gladstone. The Government do not mean to attempt to deal with the Home Rule Question. Their chief legisla- tive proposal will be a scheme of local government for Great Britain, which is predestined to failure. Here again Lord Randolph Churchill has experi- enced a personal rebuff which is quietly chuckled over by the Marshall and Snelgrove faction. Lord Randolph, who is in constant communication with Mr. Chamberlain, and whose Radical tendencies bring him under that gentleman's personal influ- ence, honestly desired to deal thoroughly with the question of local government. He would have ap- propriated bodily the Liberal scheme which Mr. Chamberlain and Sir Charles Dilke worked out to- gether, and which according to custom was left in the pigeon-holes of the Local Government office when the Liberals went out. But Marshall Snel- grovism has here also proved triumphant. Mr. Chamberlain's bill was based upon purely elective principles. The Government bill is a compromise between the necessity of the hour and old Conserva- tism, being partly elective, but heavily handicapped by fancy franchises devised in the interests of property. It is quite possible that this is the rock on which the Government will come to grief. I hear of a colossal newspaper libel case in pre- paration. The plaintiff is Mr. Frank Harris the new editor of the "Fortnightly Review." The complaint is that he has been charged with being the author of "The Radical Programme," a libellous statement, inasmuch as he is also the editor of an extreme Tory evening paper, called the "Evening News." The " Pall lall Gazette" is, as a matter of course, one of the defendants. But there are in addition not less than seventy country papers against which actions have been taken. The aggregate of dam- ages claimed amount to not less than .EllO,OOO. It has always seemed to me a pity that there is not in existence some authoritative power which could restrain eminent men from damaging their own reputation. It is extremely hard for a man who has for something like three score years lived , in the breath of public applause to admit his natural failure of his creative powers. But the duty should not be oast upon him personally. There ought to be a statutory right on the part of his near relatives or most intimate friends by which they could forcibly restrain him from tampering with his established reputation. For more than a dozen years Lord Tennyson has been sorely in need of such kindly care. He has written much that will last as long as the language. But he is not content to leave his reputation to rest on the accomplish- ments of his early manhood, and from time to time issues new poems which are feeble buTlesques on the style of the author of "The Idylls of the King" and "In Memoriam." Perhaps nothing he has done of recent years is quite so bad as his latest effort. If the issue were not authenticated by the name of an eminent and respectable firm of publishers, it might reasonably be suspected that some wag had been making merry at the expense of the Poet Laureate. What is to be said of a couplet like this— I mveelf have often babbled, doubtless of a foolish nest; Babble, babble; our old ngland may go down in babble at 1 or that other line in which Edith is sung as Feminine to ber inmost heart, and fernEine to her tender feet. I suppose this is the first time in serious poetry that the heroine's "tender feet" have been hymned. It is all very sad, and the most comforting reflection in connection with it is that we may still retain our original editions with Locksley Hall undiluted, and that his ludicrous annexe will nct find a place in 'permanent editions if Tennyson's works. . A movement is 17"10W on foot at the Reform Club which is watched with mixed feelings. It is sug- gested that a subscription should be raised to pur- chase a portrait of _Mr. Blight,which is to be placed in the saloon as a companion to that of Mr. Cobden. Two years ago such a suggestion would have been received with acclamation, and the necessary num- ber of guineas would have been supplied in the course of a week. Ido not doubt that the money will be forthcoming now, and for a sufficient reason. The springing of the suggestion at the present junc- ture is nothing more than a challenge. Mr. Bright has taken up an attitude towards the majority of the Liberal party and their leader which is one of open hostility. Circumstances have during the last ten -years so far withdrawn Mr. Bright from active participation in political affairs, that it would have been the easiest thing in the world for him to have preserved a neutral attitude at the Present junc- ture. But he has done something worse than if he had assumed an oppressive opposition. His reply to invitations from Dissentient Liberals to come over and help them Was reiterated on the occasion of their meeting the other day. He will, be says, not take pa-t in the meetings, because if he did he must say something that would be detrimental to Mr. Gladstone—that is, so absolutely inassailable is his own position, that if he only opened his mouth Mr. Gladstone and nine-tenths of the Liberal party would be demolished. This, I have reason to know, is a mode of procedure that is particularly offensive to Mr. Gladstone. If Mr. Bright has any- thing to say it would be much better to say it than to hint at it. The feeling created by this incident acutely divides the Reform Club, and many mem- bers will withhold the guinea which a shoretime ago they would gladly have given. But the Whig section of the club, now lost in admiration for the former object of its suspicion, is bound to carry the matter through, and we shall certainly have the portrait.

LIBERALISM IN COUNTRY PLACES. Sir,—" W. G." does well to call attention to the indiffer- ence displayed by the great lights and leedere of the Liberal party to the claims of country districts. The inhabitants of country districts are not so much occupied as are the in- habitants of a town; their minds- are more at liberty to alight on any passing event. The means of acquiring infor- mation are not so easy as they are in a town, consequently any event about to happen, or any subject introduced amongst them, will occupy their minds and understanding, and probably produce a greater impressien than it wout4 in a town. With "W. G." lam firmly persuaded that here is a wide field of labour which has been sadly neglected. This ' field is neglected to a lamentable extent during the interval between elections. At these times the candidate goes round attended by several of his friends, more or less promi- nent on account of their eloquence and ability. The ques- tions placed before the electors require time for considera- tien ere they can give their decision at the polling booth. Now, I contend, that had these questions been introduced to them by A systematic course of lectures, delivered by an in- dividual competent and able to treat the questions in a pro- -per manner, and kept continually before them, they would be more able to give a decision at the pelt. The Conservatives are alive to all this, and the habita- tions of the Primrose League, which are e-tablished in most villages and out-of-the-way places, form a means of influ- encing the minds of the rural populace, and inoculating them with Conservative teachings. Now, I think we should not disdain to follow tke example set us by our opponents. If we wish to regain the position we have lost, and be pre- pared for the next general election, something must be done to educate the rurai districts, and place prominently before them the principles and teachings of the Liberal party. I think if the suggestion thrown out by " W. G." was to be adoptad, and carried out, it would be a means of "reversing the recent Liberal defeat." I trust that this suggestion will attract the attention of those whose iefiuence in the ranks of the Liberal party is felt, that they, adopting it, will give their powerful support in carrying it out, which would meet ; with the support and sympathy of many who desire to re- gain the laurels we have lost, in the ranks of whom may be found, yours respectfully, I Padgate: December 6th, 1880.

CONJURING V. SPIRITUALISM.

Sir,—l was in Warrington a day or two ago, and a friend was kind enough to give me copies of sour valuable paper, in which appears some correspondence on the above sub- j,ct. lam very much struck with the very able and eru- dite letter of " Clifford Dix." He writes with the author- ity of ore who knows, and it is nothing less than presump- tious on the part of any thick-headed and credulous spiritualist, to think—much less of attempting—to teach him anything. Indeed, when a mar, is learned up it is as futile to attempt to teach him anything as it would be to try to get a quart of thick porridge into a pint pot. For the information of your correspondent "Beta," I would politely suggest that he always wait till "pots" of this kind become snipped, cracked, or knocked over—anyway, so long as they lose some of their contents—and he may then help to re-supply them. One cauuot help admiring men of such free thought as "Clifford Dix," especially when their free thinking becomes .so free that they think nobody thinks but themselves. It is admirable to notice, how they freely reason out their own beginning and their end, and prove how nothing else had a beginning, and how nothing else will end. They dilate loquaciously on the in- destructibility of matter and force, and then " stut " when they talk about spirit. However, there is this to be said, when everybody has turned Spiritualist but "Clifford Dix," he will enjoy the enviable position of being the only sensible man left. Had ' I been trying to instruct a man who was ignorant, I should have recommended him not to arrive at foregone conclusions, but to adopt the more modern method of inductive philo- sophy. Any fool may say a thing and prove it his own way ; but a scientific mind like that of " Clifford Dix " be- hives first and proves after. I would not like to judge him weongly and I hope he will not misunderstand me. • Perhaps, after all, if" Clifford Dix "could secure an intro- duction to Professor Crookes, one of the —if not the most eminent physicist of the day ; to Mr. S. C. Hall, F.S.A., editor of " The Art Journal," Mr. Alfred Russell Wallace, the great naturalist, or to Mrs Emma Hardline Britten, translator and editoress of " Art Magic," authoress of "American Spiritualism " " Nineteenth Century Miracles," itc., he might condescend to change his mind after he had discovered that two or three Spiritualists were not such " yokels " as he stems to imagine all of them to be. 1 I have met a.few learned-up men in my day, but every- . one when pricked proved to be a " wind-bag."—Yours truly, PE FER LEE.
Freehold-stt eat, Rochdale, Dec. 13th, —lBB-C.

Sir,—When a man ban to resort to gambling: to defend his cense, there is then a sign that argument and intelligence are entirely exhausted. If Mr. Acton desires to investigate the question of Spiritualism be has the means at his com- mand. Pbeis so full that he can hold no other knowledge, then we have found the perfect man. I will leave Mr. Acton with the old adage that the more a man knows the more be finds there is to know, and the less be thinks of him- self.

Just one more word to " Clifford Dix ;" then we have finished. He represents Mr. Wallis as stying that the whole of what we hear, see, feel, and smell, or touch is not real. Mr. Wallis did not say so. He said that the phenomena which cause in us the sensations of sight, hearing, smell, or feeling was admitted, but it was ceutended that it was not the eye which sees. the ear which hears, and so on with all the senses, those organs being but tee means to the end, the reality behind the teases, which receives the sensation and cognises its purport beittg the spirit, which is therefore at the least as real as the sensations it experiences. Our perceptioss do not explain our intelligence. It is our intel- ligence alone which explains our perceptions. " Clifford Dix " also makes a comparison between Mor- moniein and Spiritualism, and affirms that Mr. Wallis mis- represented the re-appearance of Jesus. Mr. Wallis claimed the re-appearance of Jesus in a materialised form (which was tangible to the senses of the apostles, and yet entered a closed room and again disappeared) was proof that it was a spiritual manifestation, and not the old flesh and blood body, else bow could it enter a room which was carefully closed for fear of the Jews ? JeFtlB wished them to understand he was not a phantom, but a temporary materialization. Many Spiritualists, myself among the rest, have witnessed similar , phenomena where in a closed bultud room with a number of perenns present, an additional form has appeared, which has afterwards disappeared, yet tangible and substantial while it lasted.

" Clifford Dix " speaks without knowledge when he save, " Spiritualists have thrown over the Chris. then God and the Christian book, and have not the courage to say se." Surely •he is measuring out corn in his own bugled. The Spiritnelists claim the right to exercise private judgment regarding the Bible, and to interpret it according to the light within them, and ip the light of their experience. As to the Christian God, 14 were not aware the Christians had a God of their own. If they have, then. the Spiritualists reverence, love, worship the God of the universe, who is a Spirit, and must be worshipped in spirit and in truth. "Clifford Dix" further save Mr. Wallis had learned his lesson well, and thus shows his anitnus. Unable to credit us with honesty, but assuming superior righeousuess, he, the self-appointed criqC in a matter of which he admits himself ignorant, condemns it as "humbug," solely because he does not understand the facts of the subject. Let me tell Mr. Dix that Mr. Wallis did not know what was the subject which had been advertised (which was selected by myself, not by Mr. Wallis,) until a few minutes before go- ing on the pletforrn, and therefore had he been so minded, could have had but little time to learn his lesson or prepare his arguments. But when "Clifford Dix" wishes to learn, and will seek the knowledge as an earnest and impartial. truth-seeker should, in an open and candid spirit, then I will do my best to kelp him. Until then let him suspend his judgment," is all I ask in simple JUSTICE.
THE LIBERAL UNIONISTS IN CONFERENCE. Sir,--No doubt your readers have seen from the papers that the Liberal Unionists had a Conference in London last

week, and that amongst the gentlemen lending their pre- sence to that assembly of wealth, intelligence, drc., were the names of Mr. F. Monks and Mr. William Long as re- presentatives from this district. Now, sir, I want to know by the authority of whom did these gentlemen profess to give their attendance on behalf of this district ? There is no Unionist Association in Warrington. Was it then IT the authority of the Council of the Liberal Association, or (more likely) the Council of the Conservative Association? The presumption of these gentlemen in representing this district eclipses the Scotch deputation as representing Nairn and Elgin, the meeting to elect which was called by private circular, to which about 40 responded, these being principally lawyers, landlords and their factors, gardeners, and blacksmiths, and ultimately the deputation appoin'ed was composed of Lord Fife's factor and the factor of Mr. J. R. Findlay. the principal proprietor of the 'Scotsman," which has "gone wrong "on the question of Home Rule. I think, sir, if these gentlemen, instead of dining sump- tuously and airing their eloquence in denouncing the mem- bers of the party which they have deraateii, and promising their support to the present Government of "law and order," were to give some study to the present condition of Ireland, and do what they have been often asked to do by the Liberal party, viz., formulate some plan which might be the means of bringirg some degree of peace to that dis- tracted country, we should not be witnessing the Govern- tnent raking up buried Acts of Parliament in order to strike at men representing popular opinion in Ireland. I refer particularly to "honest "John Dillon. Do not the revela- tions of the now famous Sligo jury panel show the parti- sanship displayed in the matter of jury packing? and yet, because a meeting was called to protest against the constitution of this panel, the meeting was proclaimed by the authorities. Nave the Catholic population of Sligo is to the Protestant population as 8 is to 1, and yet the under-sheriff for reasons partly explained by himself managed to constitute this jury panel thus-144 Protestants and 105 Catholics. In cross-exami- nation by Mr. Bodkin, who challenged the jury panel as counsel for the prisoners, this worthy admitted that the reason Catholics were ordered aside was to enable the crown ;to get convictions. Chief Baron Pallee, who heard the I challenge, uttered the following remarkable sentence, "There is no doubt that not one juror now on the panel would be ,on the panel if it were fairly and properly prepared. 1 will express no opinion on the law. lam not 'ay law entitled to quash the panel, and if I had any discretion to quash the panel, on the ground of irregularity, I would in this case exercise it without the slightest hesitation." The motion was then adjourned, and upon the next prisoner pleading guilty to a charge of larceny the Judge said he should as- sign him counsel as "owing to what had occurred in the empannelling of the jury which was to try him he could not allow him to go to the jury ignorant of his righta, and therefore unable to exercise them." After remarks like this from the Judge it is not to be wondered at that counsel for the Crown asked that all the cases might stand over to enable the Crown to decide what course they would adopt on the question of the jury panel.—Yours, Jac.,

div.head: CRISIS IN IRELAND. ARREST OF MESSRS. DILLON, O'BRIEN, AND OTHERS.
div.p: THE CRISIS IN IRELAND. ARREST OF MESSRS. DILLON, O'BRIEN, AND OTHERS.

On Thursday morning Messrs. John Dillon and William O'Brien left Dublin by mail train for Woodlawn, from whence they drove to Loughrea, where it had been for some days past announced that they intended to hold a " rent office," for the purpose of collecting the rents of the tenants of the Clanricarde estate residing in that part of Galway. , Soon after the arrival of Messrs. (.'Brier, and Dillon a meet- ing was held opposite the hotel, at which the proceedings were most enthusiastic. The chair was teken by the Rev. Mr. Cunningham, who was supported by a large number of Roman Catholic clergymen. A large force of police were present protecting a Government reporter. It was market day in Lunghrea, and there was an immense concourse of , the Clanricarde tenants present. Amongst those on the platform were Mr. Matthew Harris, M.P., Mr. David Sheehy, M.P. Mr. John Roche, poor-law guardian, Woodford, and the R4V. Father Egan. At the conclusion of the meeting a procession was formed which marched to the office of the local branch of the National League, where a rent office was opened ; but the receipt of the money had scarcely commenced when the police entered tinder the command of Mr. Davis, the district inspector in charge of the constabulary. A raid was at once made on the books and documents lying about, and the money wbich had been collected, amounting to £BB, was seized: Mr. Dillon WAS then arrested on a charge of hav- ing conspired to prevent people front doing that which they had a lawful right to do, viz , pay their rents. Mr. Dillon would not consent to give up the morie., and it was forcibly taken from him by the District - Inspector. The police proceeded upstairs to where Mr. O'Brien was collectiog rents, and arrested him, and subsequently art eeted Ms. Matthew Harris, M.P., and Mr. David Sheehy, M.P. Great excitement prevails. Subsequently Messrs. Dillon, O'Brien, Sheehy, and Harris were brought up before the resident magistrate, and a remand for a week was asked by the police. This was acc,aled to. bail being taken for the -defendants' appearance in the sum of £3O each and a suiety ! of .4.1.00.

ENGLISH HALL MARKS ON FOREIGN WATCHES.—A numerous deputation, representing the watch trade in Liver pool, Prescet, Coventry. and London, waited upon Lord Stanley of Preston and Barer. H. de Worms, M.P., at the Board of Trade, on Tuesday, in reference to the intro- duction of foreign made goods and their sale as English under the English hall mark. Amongst those present were several members of Parliament, and Messrs. Hewitt, Robin- son, and ,Berry (Prescot). Mr. A. B. Forwood, M.P., introduced the deputation. Addresses were given by Mr.. Eaton, M.P., Mr, Walker (Covestry), and others, including Mr. Hewitt. Prescot, who said the trade had bear located there for upwards of 200 years. They had within the last twenty years introduced steam machinery for the movements, which had been made upon an approved principle and to standard sizes in general use throughout the trade. The very watch Mr. Boween had shown was an imitation of theirs. It had in it a dummy piece, which would make it wind up to the left, so that the public might be deceived into the belief that it was English make. He need hardly say the joining piece was a det,i- ment to the watch. The keyless watch again we developed ts a lure extent in Prescot, ore firm 'employing 300 hands. When that firm got a repute for making thew?' watches i London agent, belonging to a Geneva firm, bought up all the sizes, took them to Geneva, and. under the present system. bad so degraded the principle that fair competition was Ampossible. And vet 'people carried about these watches believing they. were English made. He hoped the Government would endeavour to re- store an ancient industry by givinap. them a clause in the Merchandise Marks Bill which they were preparing.— Lord Stanley said he was very glad to recognise what w the general feeling of the deputation and of the trade in all parts of the country, that the rnovaruent was not one for protection against competition, but against fraud. He wished to know whether the suggestion was that the move• merits should be hall marked.—Severat members of the de- putation said they wished to prevent foreign cases from ob- taining the mark and foreign movements being put into English hall marked cases.—Lord Stanley said he was as. desirous as they were to eliminate fraud, and felt it to be his duty to do all he could legitimately in that direction. He should consider very carefully what they had said, and if in the course of legislation he found the means by which they could fairly deal with this matter without undue in- terference with trade, he should personally do his utmost to bring about legislatien.—The deputation, thanked the president and witbdreß.

THE BELFAST RIOTS—At the Omagh Assizes, on Thurs' day, a largo number of persons, convicted of taking part in the Belfast riots, received sentence. In many cases Ben- tence of seven years' penal servitude was passed, and in the remainder substantial periods of imprisonment were or- dered. Joseph Walker was put on trial for the murder of a soldier, but, as in the case of his sou tried the previous day, the jury could not agree to a verdict. On Wednesday night a crowd proceeded to the farm beld tei7 Mr. Ellis at Mynydd, Mostyn, who ordered the bailiff eff, and escorted him to the station, compelling bias to take the train for Chester. Jones's farm, ecol:ing him to Holywell. • BAPTIST BAND OF HOPE.—The members of this society paid a frielidly visit to the Good Templits' Ltdge- room, Bridge-street, and entertained the members 0 the Pride of Earlestown Juvenile Temple.
