A newspaper chronicling the wrecking of a vessel says, "The only passengers were T. B. Nathan, who owned three-fourths of the cargo and the captain's wife." AN AGED 0 7STES.--AD American eating-house keeper advertised for "a boy to open oysters fifteen yearsold.", When an oyster becomes such a veteran, its age should be kept a secret, the same as a spring chicken's. Surely an oyster ought to be able to open itself long before it reaches its fifteenth year. IT Mom' as Thaay.—Traveller : "Is this the right road to Greenville?" Rustic: "Well, er—it may be." Traveller : "It may be? What do you mean by that ? " Rustic: "'You see, if you take the right-hand road down here at the forks this is the right road, but if you are fool 'nuff to take the left-hand road then this is not the right road" In a Chinese village during a time of drought, a mis- sionary saw a row of idols put in the hottest and dustiest part of the road. He inquired the reason, and the natives answered: "We prayed our gods to send us rain, and they won't, so we've put them out to see how they like the heat and dryness." This plan might be tried on town officials. Set them in the mud of streets they will not clean. In a village not many miles from Edinburgh lived two worthies named Sandy Mc.Tavish and John Bain. They were one night sitting in the public-house enjoying a glass of the real Glenlivet, when the talk turned on politics, on which subject they" agreed to differ." The discussion got somewhat heated, and Sandy, after much eloquent abule of the statesman from whose policy he differed, thumped the table till the glasses rattled, and sly-Aited triumphantly "I tell ye, John Bain, that ye canna argue awa' facts. Facts are obstinate things." "Man, Sandy," was the canny reply, "what a great fact ye maun be !' HEARSAY EVIDENCE.—An eminent Lord Chief Justice who was trying a right-of-way case had before him a a witness—an ol d fanner—who was proceeding to tell the jury that be had " knowed the path for sixty yeer, and my feyther tould I as lie heerd my grandfeyther zay —" "Stop," said the Judge, "we can't have hearsay evidence here." "Not," exclaimed Farmer Gile.3. "Then how dust know who thy feyther was 'cept by hearsay?" After the laughter had subsided, the Judge said "In courts of law we can only be guided with what you have seen with y;.air eyes, and nothing more or less. "Oh, that be Mowed for a tale!" replied the farmer. " I ha' got a bile on the back of my neck, and I never seed 'un, but I l'e prepared to say that he's there, dang un !" This second tri,undli on the part of the witness let in a torrent of hearsay e vidence about the footpath which obtained weight with the jary, albeit the judge told them it was not testiikiony oi any value, and the farmer's party won. A lift,loi,s teAvir,v.—Henry Ward Beecher tells an amusing slio?. of a family in Indiana where he stopped over night. firVisliiiig to show off the precocity of the children the rn,;ther asked the eldest one to say grace. But the child snarled and refused. "She's a little bilious this nirnitig, but, Willie, you show Mr. Beecher what a i•*ee grace you can say." "Don't want to," shied Willle. "lie's bilious too, said the mother, so Mr. Beeelier hici-,elf asked the blessing and the meal pte2eeied. al:ter a little the hired girl brought in some pancakes that were umlerdone. "Why, Nelly's pan- cakes afe a dead failure I his morning," said the vexed hostess, "I never knew that to happen before." "Per- haps a little bilious," suggested Mr. Beecher, with a twinkle in his eye, and everybody laughed at the ap- plication. _ .

A tourist at the Corragh was strolling round the out- skirts of the camp with a party of ladies and gentlemen, when they found a man laboriously turning a windlass which hoisted from a shaft a bmlet filled with rock. The only thing remarkable about the man at the wind- lass was his hat, the crown of which was cut clear off, allowing the hot sun to pour down upon a perfectly bald head, some waggish friends having recommended this arrangement as sure to produce a crop of hair. The gentleman and his party stood watching the man toil- ing unceasingly at his heavy labour for several minutes, when the kind-hearted visitor spoke up with concern, and said, "My friend, why don't you cover up your head? This hot sun will affect your brain." "Brain, is it ?" cried the man, as he gave the windlass another creaking revolution: "If I had any brains, d'ye think rd be here puffin' up this bucket ?"

JOHN T 1 A lI'S " TFLINFONE." By Tom PIERCE COWLING. We live i' a' ay o' improvements. Tellygrafs, telly- fortes, an' sich things, coupled wi' Socialists, lies varry near revolutionised society. Things izn'd woi they wur two hundred yer ago, when th' poet wrote— They didn'd wear two guinea suits, Ner a stove-pipe hat so tall, Ner weak breawn-paper boots, Ner Sydenhamans cut too small; They didit'd wear paste diamonds then, Ner a brassy cheon for show; Fer gentlemen wur gentlemen Two hundred yer ago. Well, they're nod ladies newt', bud led that pass. Iv they wor they'd wear no suits ad o. Three or four things hesn'd improved fey th' better. Aw refer to th' so-coed improvements i' style an' conversation. Nod as aw'm beawn ta attack thad anomaly as meks soa many good- figured lasses look like crippled dromedaries. To co a parent " boss " or " missus," "th' owd fellah " or "th' owd woman," con hardly bi coed an improvement on th' owd-fashioned an' dear names o' father an' mother.

_ Th' prevalent fashions, too, scorn ta bi retrogradin' ta th' time o' Adam an' Eve. There are ta bi sin ad every concert spectacles (under yore nose, bud nod across id) az is simply demoralisin'. Even- th' stars o' fifty an moor are either geddin' varry low wages or buyin' limas cloth, ta judge bi th' way as th' bodies o' their dresses is med.

Bud awm beawn ta dogmatise. Aw Beet deawn ta tell yo' ov a new telly lone, as Jack Hall geet fixed i' his es- tablishment, an th' fost message as coom up fra th' country. He wur a grocer o' th' owd scoo, an' thowt nowt o' cuttin' a peawnd o' cheese wi' th' bacca knife, but fer o' thad, he wur no grosser ner many as bed finer fithers. When John geet th' tellyf one up, he chuckled ta hissel, an' rattled th' brass i' his pocket, till he took olle printin' Aff. He bed printed instruc- tions pud up o'er th' instrument, an' stopped till eleven thad neet, practising to ged his hand in—nod i'th' telly- fone—but th' way o' usin' id. Id wur varry gratifyin' to his feelins to hev orders sent fro' a distance, as used to be tekken to th nearest shop. Ov course,' id wur awk- ward for th' wife to ring up a dozen times a day to ax whoa he wur tawkin' to. To use his own phrase, " Sich things dozen do." One day he heerd th' bell ring, an' gooin to th' tellyfone, he gilt a country order for two gallon o' trade, an eaunce o' camphor, an thirteen nut- megs. After geddin th' articles deawn he axed for th' name. He tried three times to catch id, bud id slipped through his fingers every time, an' when he'd gin chase to id, till he could do no moore, he axed th' customer to Spell id. Tekkin a pencil i' his hand, he stopped th' telly- fone up wi' his organ o' hearing. Th' customer coed eaut " Double U." " Aye," said John," aw've getten thad." "Double 13," said the voice. " Aw've getten id !" "Well, put it down again." "Yes, go ahead." "Double U." "Aw'll double You," sed John, if aw god to th' end o' this machinery." Then in a sweet voice he said, " Aw've gettenid." "Then put id down again." "But aw've put id deawn twice." "Then put it down three times." John sighed, an, wrote it ageon. "A double D, A double D," repeated John; " thad's queer." Then he sheawted, Wod next ?" "E double 11." John immediately con- signed th' owner o'th' voice to equatorial climes ; but after stampin, reaund th' office a good many toimes, an' pooin' hauf of his whiskers ea,ut, he answered sweetly, "Go on." " Thad's all," sed th' voice. "0 wod?" "All the name:' Then John sunk deawn in his seat an' studied his paper, as wer studded wi' the followin' hieroglyphics :—u u, uu, uu,ad d, e 11. He thowt abeawt Belshazzar's feast, an' wur welly feared to stop i th' office.

When-t-if junior partner coom in he showed him th' name, an' he sed as id needed a second Daniel to decipher thad stuff. He looked at th' paper, back, front, an' edge uppa,rds, an' axed John heaw his spirits wur. They finally coom to th' conclusion az somebry hed /An hoaxin' th' owd grocer, an' they'd tek no moor notice o'th' job. When th' 'prentice coom in, heawever, they led him look at th' paper, an' he axed to hey id gin eawt, as John had heerd id. No sooner wur this done nor he sea, "Why, id's W. W. Waddell." Ther ne'er wor sich a relief, sin thad o' Lucknow. John brasted two buttons, wi' long suppressed excite- ment, an' wur so o'ercome by th' lad's sherpness, as he med him a present ov a stick o' salery theer an' then, an, spooak abeawt givin' him moor to do mornin'. Th, 'prentice allus teks th' tellyfone orders neaw.

MeV have been so far successful as to create great excitement in Pubhc.bouse circles. The modus operandt is for three men '0 enter a vault and order drink, tendering a coin requiring to be changed. This gives them an exact hereabouts of the till. Next day three knowleciAe of the Iv men again appear, one going into the vaults and the others , into the adjoining bar parlour. Whilst No. 1 is drinking in I the vaults the others ring the bell, and on the barman en- tering be room they allow a bird to escape. One hurriedly t shuts the door and holds it whilst the other is catching the bird. In the tneanwhile, the attendant being shut up with them, their accomPlice is helping himself to the money in the till. The thieves are believed to have come from some other towns. I was jaundiced all over, and as yellow as a guinea; I could not stand, I was as weak as I could be, could not eat or sleep. During these yaars I have, from time to time, consulted many prominent physicians, both in England and on the Continent, but none of them were able to give me more than temporary relief. The terrible head- aches, awful bearing down pains, and great ner- vous depression, seemed to come round with wonder. ful exactness, even when under the doctor's care. In fact I was laid up in bed from nervous prostra- tion and debility about one half the time. My liver was torpid and sluggish, and I had no appetite. Doctors called it female complaint, but could give me no permanent relief. Hearing "Warner's SAFE Cure" highly recommended, I gave it a thorough trial, and am now in good health, all the previous troubles having left me. It is now some five months since I have taken any of the SITE Cure, yet I have had no return of my old disorder, and I consider myself permanently cured. I can heartily recommend "Warner's SAFE Cure" to all ladies who have been and are afflicted with those weaknesses and trials I once endured.

Pittrs to Mt gdttor. PROPOSED RAGGED SCHOOLS IN WARRINGTON. Sir,—Kindly allow me space for a word respecting the children of the destitute poor of our town. My heart bleeds for them in their sad condition of metal and epiritaal neglect, and amid their many physical discomforts too. I have had an impression for years, deepened very much of late, that Ragged Schools are the great want of Warring- ton to train the poor children in the way they should go. At present how many are baing trained by their surround- ings in all kinds of vice and sin? At the Silver-street mission service on Sunday evenings it is heartrending to see so many half-clad children glad to gat out of the rain and cold, and it is interesting to see them joining in the singing of the sweet hymns, and listening to the words that are spoken. I fully believe if some of our well-to-do towns- people ha ti seen aad thought and felt what I have done. they would liberally help me in the purpose I have under- taken. Messrs. Naylor, J. Monnfield, and Smethurst are assisting me in seating the Dallam-lane old chapel, which may serve as a useful Protestant Ragged School, to be opened on Christmas Sand ty. I now through your columns appeal to all who are touched with true sympathy in such a practical work as this, to contribute in children's cast-off clothing, or in money, so that the work may be a lasting success. Any help that Christian feeling- will prompt, Mr. R. Dale, 53, Bewsey-street, will be pleased to receive for—Yours. &e., JAMES SICELLAND, 60, Bewsey-road. P S.—Any Christian friends who, 'are willing to help in making the meetings of the children-a success are requested to give in their names to Mr. R. Dale.

div.p: CHRISTM'AS wAt rs OR BANDS.

is of a comfort when you have a grievance, whether real or imaginary, to have a newspaper I in which you can ventilate your grievance. The approach- ing season brings with it a feature that may be variously esteemed by different individuals. I refer to the nuisance of those who think they have special gifts in the musical line, and will insist on going round to the various houses in town and neighbourhood serenading quiet people, who are frequently in bed. The hands are often composed of a dis- eased cornet, a wheezy fi igeolet. perhaps a second-hand fiddle or two, and one of those long brass things with a big mouth, worked like a pump; and just after your feet are comfortably encased in your slippers, and you have settleA down for an hour's readine, after the babies are in bed, all at once you are put into a cold sweat by hear- ing at the front door a band of these men who insist on giving you a treat. They usually give you a selection of old psalm tunes. interspersed, it may be. with "Hail, smiling morn," and if they see a good handsome silver coin, and a glass of beer behind it, they will strike up "See the, conquerine hero comes," and possibly wind up with "God save the Queen," row, I should be sorry to doubt the honourable motives o, these men, and believe,as some one pleased to say,that the money thus obtained furnishes a big supper and carouse afterwards, but am willing to think that in some cases, at least, they honestly believe that the public have very little knowledge of what good music is, and therefore after a hard day's work, out of pure motives of benevolence, they leave their own homes and families to give their neighbours a treat. Be it so: but would it not be courteous, to say the least of it, to inquire, first of all, if there is sickness in the house they propose to entertain, and to ASK, if there.is not, whether it would be agreeable to the residents to listen to their charming strains. I confess, when being dis- turbed sometimes by these unwelcome visitors at unseemly hours, I should not wonder if strong language were used and peremptory orders issued that if they valued whole skins they would be wise to carry their benevolence where it was more appreciated. I should be sorry to follow or recommend the example to my friends of what a gentle- man in Cheshire did to cure the evil, namely, to shoot at them', whereby he seriously injured and maimed one of the disciples of Handel. but I can quite underetand in many cases it causes considerable annoyance. I would sagged that as an easy way fo- them to meet difficulties of this sort for them to carry a printed card with the names and addresses of the artists, which one of them should band in at the house where they propose to play, and if permission is obtained it would be all plain sailing there. As it is. in many cases their talent is not appreciated, or only valued at a few coppers, at which the leader, who carries the bag, looks thunder, and they retire with a very bad grace, mutter- ing words which would not embellish or improve any Sun- day school hymn book.—Yours, &c., A SUFFERER.

HALTON PAROCHIAL SCHOOL.—The Diocesan inspection of the children of Halton Parochial Schools in religious knowledge has jest taken place, and the inspector has re- ported favourably of all the standards. LACEY-STREET S CHOOL : PROPOSED JUVENILE MI S- SIONARY SOCIETY.—On Sunday afternoon last what was termed the first juvenile missionary meeting was held in Lacey-street school. There was a good number of scholars present. The superintendent, Mr. B. Brown, presided. Tbe Rev. J. Bryant spoke of the great good that had been done by foreign missions. The. Rev R. Burdon also spoke of the scenes he had witnessed in the island of Trinidad where he had been stationed six years. Mr. Houghton having spoken, a collection was made in aid of the missions, which realised Se. 15s &It WIDNES WESLEYAN CIRCIIIT.—The quarterly meeting in connection with this circuit was held at Lacey-street school on Monday. The local preachers mat in the afternoon. \when Mr Bellis, of Oakland-street, was placed on fall plan. Subsequently tea was provided by Mr and Mrs S Robinson, of which a good nnmber partook. The business meeting in the evening was presided over by the Rev R Burdon, sup- ported by the Rev J Bryant. The retiring stewards, Mr Jeseph Robinson and Mr T S Swale, were thanked for their services in that capacity during the past three years, and Mr Swale and Mr S Robinson were appointed stewards for the next year. Mr J Robinson was appointed circuit chapel secretary. and Mr Stringer superintendent of the Christian Workers' Association. SIMMS CROSS BOARD SCHOOL, WIDNES.—On October the 19th 250 boys of the above school were Examined under the South Kensington Department in the first and second grades of the following subjects :—Freehand practical geometry, perspective, and model drawing. The examination was conducted by Captain Royse, of the Science and Art De- partment. The subjoined results have just ben received The boys whose exercises gained the mark " excellent " ie- calve a prize from the Science and Art Department. Num- ber of papers marked "fair," 103. Ist Grade : Freehand, 62 good ; 14 excellent. —Geometry, 43 good ; 24 excellent. Model, 20 good; 3 excellent. —Total, 125 good ; 41 excel- lent. Second Grade : Freehand, 6 good ; 1 excellent.— Geometry, 12 good ; 1 excellent.—Perspective, 1 good.— Model, 1-good ; 2 excellent—Total, 20 good; 4 excellent. The succeesful second grade scholars are : Fred. Sadler, freehand, excellent ; Frank Strinver, geometry. excellent ; Robert Bowerman and George Webb, model, excellent.

Mr. Philip Speakman, chairman of tbe Runcorn Improve- ment Commissioners, has opened a subscription list in aid of the widows and orphans of the men who lost their lives by the disasters to the Southport and St. Anne's lifeboats. Mr. E. A. Chorlton, of Parr's Back, has under.aken the duties of trea.urer, and sul,scriptions may be paid to that gentle- man. Closely identified as Runcorn is with the shipping trade, and many of its inhabitants earning a livelihood on the sea, the action of Mr. Speakman in giving the inhabi- tants an opportunity to subscribe to the sufferers needs no commendation, and a generous response will no doubt be made to his appeal.
DELAYED POLICE BUSINESS AT WIDNES.-A
MAGISTRATE'S OPINION.

The business of the Widnes Police Court has been fre- quently delayed daring the past few weeks, and even months, through the scarcity of magistrates who are availa- ble. On Thu.tday there was a most glaring instance. The summonses against the workmen who are on strike from the Public Offices to answer charges of intimidating the plas- terers now engaged upon the work were put down for hesr- log, and there were two barristers engaged in the case. Mr. Pickford represented Messrs. Tyrer, kinnon, and Co.. con- tractors, the plantiffs, and Mr. Shand appeared on behalf of the defendants. Only Colonel Gamble appeared upon the bench at the appointed time, eleven o'clock, and his Wor- ship was engaged in dealing with various small offences that only needed one magistrate to adjudicate, and with others by the consent of the parties until the arrival of Mr. Timmis about half•past twelve.—Mr. Pickford said he un- derstood that one of the magistrates was compelled to leave the court brhalf-past one, and as it would now be impos- sible to finish the case in the short period remaining, he asked that the case should be partly heard, and then be adjourned to another day at a fixed time.—Mr. C. H. Lewin (magistrates' clerk) replied that it was impossible for the two gentlemen on the beach to arrange to attend •1- gether on a fixed Cay.—Mr. Timmis said he was extremely sorry that the convenience of the gentlemen could not be consulted, and he was sorry that suitors could not have their cases decided, but he was not on the rota for that day. His partner was absent that day, and he (Mr. Timmis) had an appointment, made some time ago, to meet in Liverpool a gentleman who was travelling some hundreds of miles to keep the appointment. He always considered that he should attend to an appointment without keeping the gentle- man waiting, and he did so. Ha begged most emphatically to protest against an a rangement which made it necessary to continually call upon the lecal magistrates to di..charge the business of the court. He thought the magistrates on the rota or the clerk should make arrangements.—Mr. Lewin said he went to Liverpool purposely to get a magistrate, but was unable to get one to attend. They were all away or unable to attend. There was not one in the div-sion they could get hold of. It was not the clerk's fault.—Mr. Tim- mis : Who are the magistrates for to-day P—Mr. Lewin : Mr. Hall, who is in London, and Mr. Pilkineton.—After some conversation, it was deeded that the charges of intimidation should be heard on Monday at 1-15 p.m.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday. Mr. E. Carey occupied the chair, and there were also present—Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. S. Sadler, J. Houghton, J. Taylor, F. Heyes, W. T. Husband, R. Cook, J. Midwood, B. Brown, W. W. Gossage, D. Wright, T. Handley, J. T. Allen (clerk), T. Higginson (surveyor), L Carr (gas engineer).

div.head: QUEEN'S JUBILEE:.
div.p: THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE:.

The Chairman said a circular letter had been received from the Prince of Wales with reference to some memorial it was proposed to institute in London to celebrate the Queen's Jubilee. The chairm in said this was a matter for the ratepayers to consider, and the question whs whether a public meeting should be called to discuss it. He suggested that the matter be postponed for a month, in the absence of Mr. Gossage.—This was agreed to.

div.head: SUGGESTED SANITARY IMPROVEMENTS.
div.p: SUGGESTED SANITARY IMPROVEMENTS.

The Local Government Board wrote in reference to the recommendation contained in the memorandum of advice which their inspector. Dr. Page, left with the Widnes Urban Sanitary Authority after his recent inspection of the urban sanitary district. The Board were glad to find that the Urban Sanitary Authority recognise the importance of the several matters upon which Dr. Page hat reported. They desired,lowever, to call the attention of the Sanitary Authority to the following matters :-Ist. With regard to the need for improving their arrangements for scavenging, the Board would strongly 'urge the Sanitary Authority to take into consideration the expediency of undertaking by their own servants, instead of by contractors, the removal of refuse and of the contents of filth receptacles, in order that the frequency and regularity of removal, which is necessary in the interests of health, might be habitually se- cured. 2nd. In refere,ce to the nuisances reported to exist in connection with midden privies and the state of house yards, private streets, and back passages, the Board did not gather what action had been taken by the Sanitary Au- thority. On the proposition of Dr. O'Beeffe, seconded by Mr. Heyes, the letter was referred to a joint committee of the Health and Highway Committees.

div.head: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.

The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee stated that the quantity of water now being obtained from Stock's well was in excess of what had ever been previously pumped for a continuous period. The mean rainfall for the month had been 3.545 inches. The water in stock on the 24th Novem- ber imounted to 7,295,198 gallons. The illuminating power of the gas had averaged 17 31 candles.

div.head: ILLEGAL USE OF WATER.
div.p: THE ILLEGAL USE OF WATER.

The Gas and Water Committee recommended that a man named Jones be prosecuted for illegally using the Board's water. Mr. Brown said Jones was enaploy-d in a signal box at a railway crossing, and had been in the habit of using water from Messrs. Mnspratt and Son's works close by, for the purpose of cleaning out his cabin. The railway company said it was no part of Jones's (miners to clean oat the cabin, and if it was there was water provided. Dr. O'Keeffe characterised the action of the committee as persecution, and moved that the recommendation be ex- punged from the minutes.—Mr. Midwood seconded the mo- tion. The committee ought to serve everybody alike. He knew people who had Came into the town for years, and bad illegally taken a great deal more water than Jones had taken, and the Board had never taken action.—Mr. Brown thought there was a principle involved, and the committee ought to have tire power to protect themselves against any illegal use of water. (Hear, hear.)—The amendment was defeated by five votes to four, and the minutes were adopted. HIGHWAY comatirrim. This committee recommended that tenders be accented for the following streets :—Wellington, £657 10i ; Victoria £641 183 ; Margaret, £357 4a; Farrant, £298 ss; New, £285 us; Ellison, £353 tia; Lea, £2ll Os 9d; Fisher, £252 18s; total, £34057 12s 9d.—The Chairman moved, and Mr. Sadler seconded the adoption of the minutes, which was carried.

div.head: DANGEROUS SPCff.
div.p: A DANGEROUS SPCff.

Dr. O'Keeffe called the attention of the Highway Corn- rnittee to the necessity of having hanrirails on the bridge leading from Anne-street to Moss I34nk. The bridge be- longed to the Cheshire Lines Committee. It was in a dangerous state last year when there was snow and frost, and several accidents occurred there that might have been prevented if there had been handrails.—The Chairman said the matter should have attention.

HEALTH STATISTICS. I The Medical Officer (Dr. Cooper) reported to the Health Committee that during November there were 93 births and 37 deaths, being at the rate respectively of 40 58 and 164 pr thousand. Of the deaths 16 occurred amoust children under one year, and 10 amongst children between one and five years. Zymotic diseases caused six deaths. He called attention to the insanitary state of the following adopted streets :—Sankey-street, Water-street, Gerrard-street, off Waterloo-road, and Catherine-street. He had visited all the bakehouses in the township, and, with the exception of two, found them in a fairly satisfactory condition.

THE INFIRMARY.—The annual meeting of the Sunday Hospital Committee was, held in a room of the institution on Wednesday afternoon, when there were present the Revs. S. Wilkinson, J. Allton, J. D. Wray, Alderman Davies, Mr. Buck- ton, Mr. John Roberts, and Mr. Z. Armitage (honor- ary secretary): The total receipts from the Hospital ,Sunday collections were reported as amounting to £167 4s 2d, being a decrease of .229 us 3d on last year's collections. The Hospital Saturday collections from the various works this year amounted to £2B7' 58 7fd. . The boxes from three large works had not yet -come to hand. The contributions from those firms would probably bring the amount up to about £367, being over £lOO short of the collections of the previous year. Thk, only way, the Honorary Secretary said, in which the decrease could be ac- counted for was I through the depressed state' of trade. Mr. John Roberts was of a similar opinion, and Alderman Davies thought that, considering the difficulties that had to be encountered, the re- sult was very good indeed. The report was adopted on the motion of the Rev. S. Wilkinson, seconded by the Rev. J. Allton. . On the proposition of Mr. John Roberts, seconded by Alderman Davies,•the 27th of March, 1887, was fixed for next Hospital Sunday. This was all the business. HOLY TRINITY LITERARY AND DEBATING SOCIETY. —At a meeting of this society on Monday evening Mr. T. J..HuLse read a paper on" Railways and Rail- way Rates." Starting with a brief reference to the origin and development of railways, comparison was made bet ween•the original railway system and the gigantic one of the present day. The paper prc- ceeded with a consideration of the social results derivable from the existence of railways, from the employment of so much labour .in connection with their working. The disadvantages of the old system of trunk lines, which was quickly brushed aside by the requirements of trade, were pointed out, and mention was made of the enabling powers and terms in the Act of 1844, by which the Govern- ment is able to take over all lines which have existed 21 years, and the question of State control over railways was also touched upon. The question of railway rates was next referred to, complaints against Jthose rates being cited at length. Many of the different continental railway systems and rates were mentioned, as also were the efforts of Parlia- ment and individual statesmen to remedy the evils and defects of the system crf English railway rates. In conclusion Mr. Hulse enumerated the sugges- tions and proposals for reform which had been made, and commended the question for considera- tion. A debate ensued, and on the motion of Mr. Longton, seconded by Mr. Smithies, a vote of thanks was given to Mr. Hulse for his paper. WORKMEN'S CLUB: ANNUAL MEETING. ---- On Tuesday evening the annual meeting of the mem- bers and life governors of this club was held at the club premises in Market-place. The chair was occu- pied by Mr. J.Totter, who explained the business that the meeting was called to transact. The sec- retary, Mr. I. Leeson, read the balance sheet, from which it appeared that during the past year the total income had been £133 8s 6d; the expendi- ture left an adverse balance of .E 9 6s 33-d. It was explained that this balance was principally dtie to necessary alterations having been made. The report was adopted on the motion of Mr. Ashcroft, sec- onded by Mr. Sanson.—lt was resolved, on the mo- tion.of Mr. Ashcroft, that four vice-presidents be .elected; instead of one, as heretofore. The proposer explained that he made the proposition in view of the change that was cbntemplated. If the club was made free, as had been suggested, it would be ad- visable to have more vice-presidents.—The Chair- man moved " That in future there be no fixed num- • ber for a quorum, but any meeting called shall at the time specified proceed to be conducted by the members then present." The motion was seconded, but on being put to the vote was lost, and it was resolved that the quorum remain at seven as before. —The Chairman made a reference to the illness of the Mayor, and reported that a resolution of condo- lence in her affliction had been sent to Mrs. Mackie by the committee. The resolution referred to the Mayor's connection with the club since its fcirma- tion, the deep interest both he and Mrs, Mackie had taken-in its welfare, and the intention § Dr. Mackie had expressed with regard to the further extension of its usefulness in the coming jubilee year as tend- ing to endear him to the hearts of the members, and tointensify their grief and sympathy. The com- mittee regarded the Mayor's illneess at this juncture as a public calamity, and trustdd that he might soon be restored to health to take an active part in carrying out 'those movements which, under his guidance, gave promise of such credit and honour to the town and incalculable benefit to the present and future generations.—lt was then resolved, on the motion of Mr. Bailey,seconded by Mr. Sanson, that Dr. Mackie be re-elected President of the club. —The, committee for the ensuing year was then elected as follows : Messrs. Ashcroft, Bailey, Daniels, Dyson. Earde, Ellis, Ford, Hollingsworth, Heywood, Leeson, A. .B. Mackie, Potter, Russell, T. Sanson, W. Sanson, and Stout.—Mr. J. Potter was appointed chairman of the committee; Mr. Hol- lingsworth, treasurer; Mr. Leeson, secretary; and Mr,.Stout, assistant secretary.—This was all the business.

WESLEYAN MUSICAL FESTIVAL AT RUNCORN. The musical festival given by the choir of St. Paul's Chapel, and the scholars and teachers of Brunswick Sunday School, has become one of the most popular events in con. nection with Wesleyanism in Runcorn. The performance of Monday evening was equilly soccessful with its prede- c-esor, and the Public Hall was well filled with an apprecia- tive audience. Mr. Robert Shaw occupied the po4ition of ch iirman, and in opening the proceedings delivered a brief speech. The presence of so many people that evening, he said, was an indication of the interest they took in their young people, and he was quite sure there was nothing that ought to interest them so much. The Sunday schools ex- erted a far greater influence than the had any concaption of in connection with their peace and comfort of mind. He was sure the manager of Brunswick Sunday School had conceived a very good idea in bringing them together in a way like that. The more they could bring their young' people together and the more they could get their thoi gh s and minds wrapped up in Sunday school work, the greeter

iofluence would be exerted on their future lives. Meetin.2.3 like those would have the effect of contro'- ling and guiding them in after years, when they left their parental homes. He trusted that the presence of that audience would stimulate them; that it would deepen their sympathy te unite them mere closely to their teachers, and ultimately lead them tl become mem- bers of their churches, so that in time they might take the places of the officers who were at present labouring in their Sunday schools. Young, and the chairman tool: part. ! Csont. SUPPER.—On Monday evening the Vicar and Mrs. Wilkinson entertained the voluntary choir of St. Paul's at supper. About 60 were present. After supper, the Vicar thanked all present for the valuableihelp they had rendered during the past year, at the same time remarking that he felt sure they all considered it their pleasure as well as their duty to use the voices God had given them for His service in His own house ,of prayer. He also spoke in high terms of the services of the organist, Mr. John Lythgoe. The Rev. R. W. Samuel and the Rev. G. D. Wray (Vicar of- St. Peter's) also spoke. Afterwards a most enjoyable evening was spent. ITHE WARRINGTON HARRIERS.—Owing to the unfavourable weather on Saturday for cross-country I running only eight members turned up, namely, G. Stokes, G. Ratoliffe, A. Ratcliffe, J. Smith, J. Chrimes, T. Eden, H. 31addock, and J. Waterworth. They left the club room at 3-30,with H.Maddock as pace, and showed the way down Arpley-street and on to Walton Arches, then along the canal for about half a mile. Crossing the canal, they went down Bellhouse-lane and came on the high road. Turning to the left, they went over Tom Payne's Bridge and along Wilderspool Causeway, arriving home at 4-20, after a very pleasant run of 50 minutes. Distance about six miles. DEATH OF THE REV. E. J. HARTLAND. The Rev. Edwin J. Hartland, a well-known Congrega- tional minister, died on Sunday night at Swansea. The deceased, about twelve months ago, resigned the positions of secretary of the Congregational Churcb Aid and Home Missionary Society, and of hon. secretary of the Irish Evangelical Society, ow- ing to an affection of the heart, and went to reside with a son at Swansea. , Mr. Hartland had been re- , cently advised to.go.to Switzerland for the benefit 1 of his health; and it is presumed that the unusual excitement consequent upon his intention to start in about a fortnight accelerated his death. Mr. Hartland was a student-, at Chesnut College from 1840-44, his first pa.storate being at Chatter's in the latter year, his second at Aldermanbury, 1847; his third at Warrington, 1850; and his fourth at Bris- tol, 1855. Mr. trartland was also principal of the Bristol Congregational Institute from 1863 till 1879. Mr. Hartland had many friends in War, :ington. WIDNES COUNVII. OF EDUCATION.

The annual gathering and distribution of prizes to the school children under the auspices of the Widnes Council of Education was held in the Volunteer Hall. on Thurs Jay evening. The gallery was occupied by 650 children, selec- ted from the Board and denominational schools. and they added much to the pleasure of the crowded audience by their rendering of a number of part songs and glees under the able conductorship of Mr. J. C. Crawford. Mr.- T. S. Timmis, president of the council, occupied the chair, and he was supported on the platform by the Rev. and Mrs Wright- Williams, the Rev. :ieorge Bond, Messrs. H. Wade Deacr,n, J. Morrison, and Dr. MacLennan.—ln opening the pro- ceedings the chairman adverted to the fact that the period of three years for which the council was originally formed, was at an end. The results bed exceeded the most san- guine expectations of the council. They had two objects in view. firstly to increase the attendance of the children, and secondly to promote thrift. Money prizes were given to attain that end, and were invested in the Post Office Savings Bank in the children's names. The attend- ances of the scholars had gone up In a marked degree etch year of the coencil's existence, the present year being better than all. (Applause.) Tbe endeavour to in- culcate thrifty habits had also been attended with success, and most of the money invested had been allowed to remain in the Bank, and in very numerous instances additions had been made. Mr. Timmis announced that it had been deter- mined to make the Council of Education a permanent insti- tution, and although the subscriptions bad come in very freely from the manafacturers, they had not sufficient. and be invited any person who felt an interest in the work to aid them.—Mr. Deacon (hon. sec ) read letters from the Revs. Father Finegan and Father Clarke. who, while apolo- gising for their inability to be present, expressed high ap- proval of the labour of the council. Mr. Deacon also pre- sented the third annual report. which stated that the system of prizes and certificates, which had previously been in force, was continued, and below, in a tabular form, is given the number of children in each school who have gained the rewards : I. 11. 111. div.p: LYMM
Lyarst LIBERAL Amami:mg.—The anneal meeting of the members of the Lymm Polling District Liberal Associa- tion will be held in the Club-room, Eagle-brow. next Tues- day. .

TRAP Accumirr.—A trap accident happened at High Legb, near Lying], on Wednesday. Miss Helen Bmdburn was driving a horse and trap home-after a funeral, when one of the wheels of a passing cart caught the aide of the trap, which was upset. She was thrown out and sustained a severe shock. The horse was not injured. CO/MUTAT:WE SOIREE :—On Monday evening the annual soiree in connection with the Lymm Conservative and Con- stitutional Apociation was held in the Assembly Room, at the Plough Hotel. •Mr. P. Stubbs, vice-president of the association, who occupied the chair, in opening the proceed- ings, referred to the changes which had taken place since their last meeting in that hall twelve months age, and said be thought they had every reason to be satisfied with the position in which their locgl association now- stood. He was glad to think that the recommendation of their late IRmented member, Mr. John Brooks, that a branch of the Primrose teagae should be established in that neighbour- hood, had been carried out. (Hear, hear.) He believed that if the league was administered and carried out in the same spirit of friendliness in which it was originated it would be of great Service locally, and in the interests of the Conservative cause generally. (Applause.) Mr. J. W. Sidebotham, M.P. for Hyde Division, gave an address. Referring to the Irish question, he said that when Ireland was quietly settling down and losing its ter- rors, suddenly the Irish agitators awoke to the fact that their power was slipping from their grasp, the word went out for a campaign against rent, and the result was that Ireland at this moment was once more plunged into anarchy and confusion. (Hear, hear.) The course of the Govern- ment was perfectly clear. These Irish tenants must be made to obey the law and to pay their rents. They must teach these Irish agitators that they could not with impunity go on sowing the' seeds of dissension and discord in that unhappy land. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Let obstruction do its worst, they could deal with it, they could fight with it, and, he believed, they could in the end conquer it. (Applause.) He thought they had marked out for themselves a path of duty, and neither threats, intimida- tion, cajoleries, nor promises would cause them to swerve from it by one inch. (Applause.)—A vote of thanks was afterwards passed to Mr. Sidebotham, and a musical pro- gramme was then proceeded witb.

After years of Agony. 69, BURTON CRESCENT, LONDON, W.C.—Ever since my child was born, some seven years ago, I have suf- fered very much from uterine disorders, which have rendered me very miserable and have confined me to my bed a large portion of the time. I suffered intensely from Violent headaches, with a great deal of pain in my back, and became very much reduced in flesh and spirits. What was to me, in addition to this, a very peculiar thing, was that I gradually lost my hearing. I consulted a number of physicians in London, and one and all advised me to take a sea voyage; I did so, without deriving much benefit from it. When I arrived at New York, I consulted two of the best known physicians who make a speciality of diseases of women, and received only temporary relief from their treatment; and I came back to London wry much discouraged. A lady friend, who had been very badly afflicted in the same manner as myself, advised me to take "Warner's SAFE Cure," which she had done, and to her surprise it had effectually and rapidly cured her. I was so sick of medicine that it was sometime before I could be induced to try it, but finally I did, and after two bottles I found myself gaining flesh. I have taken eleven bottles in all, and can truthfully say that I have at last been restored to health. All the pains and aches have left me, and my hearing has gradually been restored. I can thoroughly and honestly recommend this medicine as being the best 1 in the world for women suffering as I did, and I I advise them all to take it. Should any 1 woman desire to write to me to learn more par- 1 ticulars in regard to this, I shall be happy to hear from her. Naturally prejudiced against pro- prietary medicines, it was with reluctance that I at last consented to try " Warner's SAFE Cure." The christening of Princess Beatrice's son will take place in the private chapel, Windsor Castle, to-day at one o'clock. . The ceremony will be of a private character. TRII MAIL CONTRACTS.—The 'Postmaster-General an- nounces that the agreements now in force for the convey- ance of mails from this country to the United States will expire on the 28th February next, and that he is prepared to receive, at once, tenders for the performance of the service after that date. Tni TITER AGITATION.—Fifty farmers within a radius of ten miles of Andover having petitioned for a reduction of 25 per cent, from tithes, which has been refused, have at a meeting at Andover yesterday decided not to pay any more tithes. A fund has been started to cover expenses in case of distraint. -Mr. tlfred Butterworth, landowner, sub- seabed £lOO. BURIED INSTEAD or Mannurn.—On Friday morning, James Makin, twenty-one years of age, a member of the St. Helens.contingent of the Salvation Army, who was to have been married on New Year's Day, was killed in Ashtons Green Colliery. Makin and his father, and another man sat down to rest, a fall of roof occurred, young Makin was buried, and when extricated a quarter of an hour afterwards, life was extinct. The other two narrowly escaped. HEAVY DAMAGES AGAINST A RAILWAY COMPANY.—III the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Justice, yesterday, Mr. Simon Elkan, a tobacco and cigar merchant, of London and Birmingham, sued the Great Northern Railway Company to recover damages for personal injuries sustained through an accident on the defendant company's line at Doncaster, which had, it was alleged, such an effect upon the plaintiff's health that diabetes supervened, and he was unable to attend to his business. The Judge found for the plaintiff. damages £3,750, for which judgment was given, with costs. DARING RAILWAY ROBBERY.—A-most daring and skilful robbery was cominitted On the railway near Radcliffe, Lan- cashire, on Friday morning. Mr. John Heap, cashier to Messrs. Knowles and Sons. Radcliffe, was travelling to Rad- cliffe with over £6OO, the wages for the men at the wcrks,in a leather bag, when two men entered the carriage at Clif- ton Junction, having in their possession a bag similar to Mr. Heap's. During the journey from Clifton to Kingsley- road Station the bags were exchanged, and the robbers got i'cle(ar away with the bag containing the money. The other bag was found to contain iron nails. Tint CAMPBELL DIVORCE CASE.—Friday was the 16th day of Campbell divorce case. The proceedings commenced somewhat later than usual, as the jury first proceeded to Cadogan-place to experiment upon a keyhole, through which the witness O'Neill alleged that he raw Lady Colin and Captain Shaw committing adultery. On taking their places in court, the jury announced that they were agreed that it was impassible to see through with the dinner wag- gon against the door, and therefore their experience was opposed to the evidence given by Neptune Blood, Lady Colin's brother. Mr. Finlay concluded; his address just before five o'clock. Sir Charles Rusin!' will follow to-day, and the case will be concitided on Monday.'

BARD OF KINDNEES.—An entertainment under the auspices of the Earles own branch of the Band of Kindness was given in the old Primitive School,oorn, Leigh-rtreet, on Thursday evening. An enjoyable programme of recitations, 4kc.was gone through. ,_ CHARGH OF FAL93 PBETENCES.—At the Liver- pool Quarter Sessions, on Monday, John Fitzpatrick (22), ' labourer, pleaded guilty to having, at Earlestown, on the 29th tilt, attempted to obtain 5d by false pretences from William Platt. The particulars of the case have been pre- viously reported, and the prisoner was committed to gaol for two months. TERRIBLB RAILWAY FATALITY.-011 Thursday night, a shocking fatality occurred on the railway near Rainford Junction. James Grimsbaw, an elderly man, living in Lord's-row, Rainford, and employed as a collier at the Rain- ford Collieries, was going over a level crossing Oh hie way to the collieries, hen be was struck by a passenger train from St. Helens. He was knocked down, and the train passed over deceased's body, which was literally cut in two. The remains were removed to the Rainford Junction Hotel to await the inquest.
